description: The purpose of this grouped project (the project) is to replace the traditional practice of rice cultivation with System of Rice Intensification (hereafter referred as SRI) technique and thus reducing the methane generation. SRI technique helps the farmers to increase the yield with use of less water resources. The land to be cultivated under the project activity has been under traditional paddy production and would have continued with traditional practices in the absence of the project activity. The SRI technique helps the farmers to practice agriculture in sustainable manner, enhance water management practice in rice cultivation and uplift the socio-economic status of native rural. The Project instance (hereafter referred as project activity) involves the implementation of SRI technique to mitigate methane emission from paddy fields in Bodhgaya and Manpur blocks of district Gaya in Bihar state, India. The total area under the project activity for SRI is 500 hectares.

The project activity is located in the Indian state of Punjab aims at developing a unique soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration project with an objective of addressing the severe crop residue burning -air pollution issue.The project activity integrates the adoption of Sustainable Agricultural Land Management (SALM) practices.The project ensures, nutrient recycling, carbon sequestration, water conservation, weedicide savings, improved yield, climate resilience of crops and lastly change in farmer’s behaviour which is the major reason for burning. The Project activities are carried out and monitored according to approved VCS methodology VM0017: “Adoption of Sustainable Agricultural Land Management”.

This project activity aims at improvement of agricultural practices such as crop residue management and enhanced cropping practices that sequester soil organic carbon ( while increasing productivity in three different states of India . Th e farmers involved in this project activity are largely composed of small and marginal farmers having land holding sizes of 1 2 hectares . As a result, these farmers are highly susceptible to variabilities arising from the agricultural produce markets and the weather conditions The condition prior to the project implementation of the croplands in th e project area which include usage of synthetic chemical fertilizers, heavy tillage and no crop residue management.

India is one of the world's largest producers of rice and exporter of rice in the world. Rice cultivation is the most important agricultural operation in India, not only in terms of food security but also in terms of livelihood and plays a major part in the economy. It is a known fact that rice fields emit methane into the environment that contributes to global warming. The project plans to promote improved water management practices in rice cultivation instead of using the traditional practice of continuously flooded irrigation. AWD/DSR are proven methods to reduce methane emission by as much as 48% compared to flooded conditions where large amounts of methane (CH4) gets generated because of anaerobic decomposition. This project is expected to generate important co-benefits of reducing water usage during rice cultivation, decrease pest and disease attacks, improve soil health etc. Further they are also beneficial for reduced cost of cultivation for small land holders. In the first instance, the project is planned to be implemented in 8,112 hectares in Punjab and Haryana States. During the project implementation, relevant technical training and advisory was provided for the farmers to help them conduct AWD/DSR during rice cultivation. The total GHG emissions reductions due to the implementation of the project activity is estimated to be 380,225 tCO2e over 7 years.

The Agricultural Land Management project in the state of Karnataka, India aims at eliminating the dependence on chemical fertilizers by replacing it with environment friendly organic-based soil amendments. The project involves active participation of various Organic and Natural farming groups. The project activity aims at increasing the capacity of the soil to sequester carbon and enhance nutrients through adoption of sustainable management practices such as agro-forestry, mulching, green manure, vermicomposting etc. The project also holistically aims at achieving sustainable management practices which not only reduces greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions but also bring improvement to farmer livelihood and entire rural ecosystem.

The purpose of the Project is to implement a water saving technology, Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD), in the irrigated rice paddies of smallholder farmers in the climate vulnerable districts in the central Indian state of Madhya Pradesh.

The proposed VCS ALM (Agricultural Land Management) project activity aims at developing a carbon sequestration project funded by Godrej Agrovet Ltd. (GAVL) in the watershed areas of Barwani district, Madhya Pradesh in collaboration with NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development) Integrated Watershed Development Programme (IWDP). The project integrates adoption of Sustainable Agricultural Land Management (SALM) practices in the context of watershed development (as per NABARD WDF Guidelines) activities. The project is implementing on the five village watersheds viz Mansoor, Mohaliya pani, Sidri, Sulgaon and Wajhar of the Niwali Block of the District, Barwani, which is the part of the major River Kajalmata and comes under the ‘Kajalmata Watershed Project’. The identified watershed villages are most suitable for the project activity (SALM Farming) intervention as it is reported with extensive agriculture activities, but with high levels of soil erosion & degradation and falls under the IX th Agro climatic regions i.e. Western Plateau and Hills. The project activity achieves Godrej’s (Godrej Agrovet Ltd. GAVL), sustainability goal of ‘Good & Green by 2025’ which ensures the carbon neutrality and water positivity as the target’s needs. The project is implementing through in active participation with the NGO AKRSP(I) (AGA KHAN RURAL SUPPORT PROGRAMME (INDIA)), the concerned Project Implementing Agency (PIA) for the SALM project implementation in the watershed areas. The estimate of annual average GHG reductions and removals through adoption of SALM practices in the agricultural landscape is 23154 tCO2e and for the first renewal crediting period of 20 years the total reductions estimations are 463074 tCO2e. The Project activities are carried out and monitored according to approved VCS methodology VM0017: Adoption of Sustainable Agricultural Land Management.

This Project is intended to promote a range of agricultural management practice changes targeted at increasing soil organic carbon (SOC) storage and reducing net emissions of CO2, CH4, and N2O from farms across North-Western Europe. Indigo Ag helps farmers to implement climate-smart practices through an integrated system of extension and outreach, modeling, agronomy support, and digital data collection tools. Practice changes target fertilizer use, tillage, crop rotations, cover cropping, and livestock management. Beyond climate benefits, the Project will increase farm resilience to weather and climate change, promote diversity of the soil microbiome, and increase rural incomes.

The Heavy Impact Carbon Farming Program of Lithuania is a joint initiative between UAB Heavy Finance (HF) farmers within the Lithuanian Republic borders. The program utilizes private capital to implement, and adopt sustainable land management in agriculture for a long-term period, thus changing the mindset establishing climate change mitigation and biodiversity-friendly practices. It is a first-of-its-kind program in Lithuania and the Baltics. It aims to assist farmers in overcoming barriers that prevent adopting sustainable land management practices by providing scientific knowledge, training, and technical and financial support for the successful adaptation of mitigating climate activities. The program is designed to expand over time and cover a range of conservational farming practices in Lithuania to help drive the change from the current conventional agriculture toward resilient and sustainable agrifood systems.

Paddy fields are the most dominant anthropogenic sources of methane to the atmosphere (5-20% of the total emission from all anthropogenic sources ). Anaerobic decomposition of organic material in flooded rice fields produces methane, which escapes to the atmosphere primarily by transport through the rice plants. The annual amount of CH4 emitted from a given area of rice is a function of the number and duration of crops grown, water regimes before and during the cultivation period, and organic and inorganic soil amendments. Soil type, temperature, and rice cultivar also affect CH4 emissions. This CH4 emission-intensive cultivation method will be targeted by the proposed programme, that will involve the implementation of the technology/measures that result in reduced anaerobic decomposition of organic matter in rice cropping soils and thus reduced generation of methane. The project activity comprises of grouped projects of rice fields implementing the following methods: (a) Rice farms that change the water regime during the cultivation period from continuously to intermittent flooded conditions and/or a shortened period of flooded conditions; (b) Alternate wetting and drying method (AWD) (c) Rice farms that change their rice cultivation practice from transplanted to direct-seeded rice (DSR). Thus, the measure will consist of AWD and/or DSR in combination with adjusted water management system in rice cultivation.

Agrisolero farm is located in Solero e Quargnento, Alessandria in Northern Italy. The coordinates are attached as a KML file. Several agricultural practices will be implemented or modified on the land. Taken together, the goal is to reduce the carbon emissions currently emitted by this farm and raise the carbon stored in the soil. In addition, the selected measures will contribute to improving crop yields and soil health. To do so, the following methods will be applied on site; reduced amount of inorganic fertilizers,an improved fertilizer application, reduced tillage, application of organic digested fertilizer, improved water management, the use of cover crops and a reduced use of fuel. The sectoral scope 14 – Agriculture Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU) is applicable to the project. Within this sector, this project has been developed under the scope of the methodology for improved agricultural land management (VM0042 VCS methodology). The project has been found eligible under the scope of the VCS program as it meets all requirements established by the program. The crediting period chosen for this project is of 33 years, renewable 3 times. The period lasts from the 1/6/2022 to the 1/6/2055. We estimated that 55tCO2/year will be stored in the soil or not emitted.

Germany's image as an industrialized country is dominated by vehicle and machinery manufacturers as well as producers of chemical products. The agricultural use of more than 50% of the country's land area is usually overlooked, although here too, successful industrial cultivation is predominant. Technical progress in fertilizers and pesticides, agricultural machinery, and cultivation methods, as well as advances in breeding and the yield-oriented transformation of agricultural landscapes have increased yields many times over in the last 100 years. However, an accompanying effect of this growth is a significant impact on the environment and the climate. To reduce this impact while maintaining high yields, the Future Soils and Sustainable Farming Initiative aims to promote IALM (improved agriculture land management) practices in Germany. Designed as a grouped project under the VCS, the initiative’s purpose is to encourage interested farmers to participate who meet the requirements. As its initial instance, the initiative starts with a farm located southeast of Berlin in the state of Brandenburg. By applying regenerative practices, the participating farmers do not only support the global efforts to mitigate climate change by reducing and removing GHG, but also make their own soils more resistant to upcoming challenges such as longer periods of droughts or extreme weather phenomena. Furthermore, a significant contribution is made to the conservation and promotion of biodiversity.

This project encompasses the Pampas grasslands (known as La Pampa in Spanish and Os Pampas in Portuguese), which are vast grassland plains spread across the South American lowlands of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay over 750,000 sq. km. These are natural grasslands where livestock production is the key livelihood activity in the region. These grasslands are subdivided into 3 distinct ecoregions: the Uruguayan Savanna, the Humid Pampas and the Semiarid Pampas. Like other grasslands across the globe, these grasslands are under tremendous pressure from anthropogenic activities such as overgrazing and unsustainable grassland management activities. Grasslands in this region are also declining steadily due to changes in land use - the conversion of grasslands to croplands. Overgrazing and land use change has resulted in the decline of Soil Organic Carbon (SOC) across the grassland region. The project promotes sustainable grassland management activities that will both improve SOC in the soil and improve the livelihoods of the communities utilizing these ranches, directly through the carbon credit payments, which provide an additional source of income, and indirectly through the increased productivity of their lands. The regenerated lands also become much less likely to undergo land use change, because the ranchers are better able to sustain their livelihoods. This in turn ensures that crucial habitats for the flora and fauna of the region are protected.

Methane emissions through flooded rice cultivation is one of the largest sources of methane into the atmosphere. Approximately 15-20% of annual total methane emissions come from the paddy fields. Methane is a potent gas with a Global Warming Potential (GWP) of 28 is significant gas in the context of climate change. Therefore, it is essential to address the methane emissions from the rice farming to mitigate climate change. The proposed project activity aims at the reducing methane emissions from the paddy cultivation. The project has introduced direct seeded rice (DSR) technique to irrigated rice cultivation. Prior to the project activity, rice was cultivated in conventional manner with flooding of paddy farms for at least 100 days.

U.S. Farmers and Ranchers represent one of the most scalable and cost-effective solutions to draw down greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and address climate change. Arva Intelligence is a producer-first, B Corporation that uses machine learning (ML) and precision agriculture to optimize sustainable practices and profitability for landowners. Arva was founded on the principle of helping farmers and their suppliers make data-informed agronomic decisions, resulting in improved environmental stewardship for the buyers and an increased efficiency in grower operations. Limited access to data and financial risk concerns have been common barriers to adopting regenerative land management practices in the U.S., and the Arva Carbon Ready USA project will bring tools to farmers and ranchers to help them overcome barriers to adoption. Arva provides solutions through its measurement, monitoring, reporting, and verification platform and will provide its cloud-based, ML-enabled software to collect, integrate, and validate data from the adoption or expansion of on-field regenerative agricultural practices. Access to low-cost, scalable, agricultural carbon offsets is limited by the industry’s disaggregated digital infrastructure. Arva’s established Carbon Ready program allows farmers to upload field boundaries and run scenarios to determine the GHG emission values for practice changes that result in GHG avoidance/reduction and soil organic carbon sequestration. A project goal is to help growers identify the practices and seed best suited for their land and to overcome scalability challenges. To facilitate the collection of soil carbon measurements and verify location, Arva will utilize its newly developed mobile app. The project is designed as a grouped project within the USA. Arva estimates that this project will result in the removal and/or avoidance of 1,000,000 tons CO2e annually by 2023. Total GHG ERRs after the first 20 years of the project are estimated at 17,020,002 tons CO2e.

This project helps pastoralists in deploying practices that contribute to the sustainable development of the Savanna grasslands of East Africa. The pastoralists of this region have largely resorted to implementing traditional grassland management methods on their lands. The grazing of grasslands by both livestock and wildlife is widely prevalent, and degradation of land due to overgrazing is a prominent issue. In this context, the opportunity to introduce improved grassland management practices, including sustainable grazing practices, will significantly help the grasslands of the region and restore carbon to their soil, creating carbon removals while improving overall soil health. In this project, pastoralists will be mobilized to take up a variety of improved grassland management practices. These practices are proven ways to increase soil organic carbon, prevent further degradation of the grasslands, and enable pastoralists to improve their productivity.

The project intends to generate additional income to the small holder farmers of Indo- Gangetic plain region for adopting improved agricultural practices such as Zero tillage/Reduced Tillage farming, cover cropping, farm residue incorporation, and efficient water management which provide a potential to not just prevent emissions into the atmosphere but also create carbon sinks through sequestration of carbon back into the soil. The project will be a grouped project under the rice-wheat cropping system. The project considers 2019 as the baseline year in which the interventions started. Starting with 40,709 Hectares and 7,461 farms, for the first instance, the project will progressively expand to more farms in future instances following rice-wheat cropping system in Punjab (PB) and Haryana (HR) covering total area of 0.8M Hectares (8,15,864 ha) by 2029 and will be maintained until 2039.

The CIBO Initiative for Scaling Regenerative Agriculture is a holistic effort to provide financial and technical support to US commodity crop growers that results in their adoption of improved agricultural land management practices and, consequently, greenhouse gas emissions reductions and removals. CIBO’s proprietary remote sensing technologies and process-based crop and soil model (SALUS), combined with technical and financial support from both CIBO and other enterprise partners, provide the incentives, safety net, and guidance that growers across the midwestern Corn Belt region of the United States need in order to overcome the barriers to widespread adoption of improved agricultural land management practices.

Orizon’s CarbonCrop Programme supports and incentivizes South African farmers/landowners in the transition towards more sustainable agricultural practices by paying out a majority share of the carbon credit revenues resulting from emission reductions and carbon sequestration on our participating project fields. Together with our partners, we support our farmers by providing tailored financial and practical advice, building online tools to assist farmers in their transition, hosting information sessions/webinars and contributing to local research on sustainable agriculture. The program, with its project boundaries being the geographic boundaries of the Republic of South Africa, will be registered as a grouped project under VM0042 - Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management. Each project activity will be carried out and monitored according to this methodology and its supporting methodologies, standards, and tools. Over time this project will include various types of farming practices /land types by adding instances that meet the additionality and applicability conditions as per the methodology. Our vision is to be a comprehensive partner for our current and future farmers in their regenerative journey, support further research and investment into Regenerative Agriculture (“RA”) and to ultimately help drive a national shift to improve soil health and productivity to secure the long-term future of agriculture in South Africa.

The Project is designed to expand over time and cover a range of farming activities in South Africa to help drive the change from the current common conventional agricultural practices towards resilient and sustainable agricultural systems.

The Kruger to Canyons Rangeland Restoration Project is a grouped project located in the globally significant Kruger to Canyons Biosphere Reserve. The area has lost soil carbon due to unrestricted animal movements and high grazing intensities leading to low productivity and bare ground, while this is exacerbated by unfavorable herd structures. Unrestricted grazing is occurring due to a ‘tragedy of the commons’ where communal areas are over-utilized for livestock grazing and knowledge of sustainable grazing practices have lapsed. The project aims to reverse historic rangeland degradation on communal rangelands by introducing rotational grazing through herding and improved animal husbandry, and removing and reducing Greenhouse Gases in the process. Furthermore, project participants will benefit from improved access to livestock markets.

The project includes both revegetation techniques in and around agricultural land, on different lands of the Republic of South Africa, providing resilient systems to protect the agricultural land from extreme weather events. The project proposes both the IALM and ARR methodologies together, at different GIS delineated areas on each project instance (land), the agricultural methodology will incorporate regenerative agricultural practices as well as circular use of by-products from the farm, as well as neighbouring farms. The ARR compartment of the project will include revegetation of native flora around the farm, facilitating ecological resilience to the project instance and sustaining pollinators throughout the year. This will be scaled to vegetation unit specific revegetation activities and regenerative agricultural practices as applicable per the Improved Agricultural Land Management methodology of the Verified Carbon Standard. This project intends to look at the system instead of looking on how to apply a methodology onto the land, a larger look at biota and their interaction in applied stewardship. The first project instances occur in the Western Cape province, Southern Cape area of Knysna where a matrix landscape of Fynbos (ever-green shrubland, indicative of Mediterranean climates) and Temperate Forest was found historically.

A wide-ranging collaborative initiative between Ruuts and Anthesis (formerly the Climate Neutral Group (CNG)), designed to channel Carbon Offset revenue to ruminants (mainly cattle and sheep) farmers that adopt regenerative agricultural practices such as improved grazing practices in the South American agricultural space in Argentina, Chile and Paraguay and potentially neighboring countries in the near future.

The purpose of this grouped project (Program) is to replace the traditional practice of flooded irrigation (baseline) with System of Root Intensification (SRI) technique in rice cultivation (project). SRI is an intermittent wet and dry technique of cultivation which induces positive socio-economic and environmental impacts by reducing water consumption and increasing crop yield compared to baseline. This also results in reduced GHG emission emissions associated with energy use in water pumping and methane avoidance associated with standing water in farm fields compared to the baseline. Increase in yield and reduced water and energy consumption also yields socio-economic benefits to the farmers. The first project activity instance (VPA) under the program is located in the state of Odisha in India. In the baseline, farmers were using traditional agriculture practice of rice cultivation and replaced it with SRI in the project activity. The area covered in this VPA is up to 500 hectares. In the project activity, emission reductions happen due to methane avoidance from the farm fields and reduced electricity consumption. However, emission reductions due to methane avoidance alone, are being claimed under the program. It is estimated that 60,000 tCO2e of emission reductions will be generated per annum.

Alternate-wetting and drying (AWD) has been identified as one of the promising water management technologies that can correct the inefficient water use in irrigated rice ecosystem, hence conserving water for irrigating more rice fields. It uses a simple tool called an observation well, which guides farmers on the timing and depth of irrigation water to apply. This can save irrigation water up to 30% at the field level without yield penalty. The periodic (or intermittent) aeration of the subsoil also reduces methane emission emanating from decomposing organic matter that occur in flooded rice fields. Emission reductions are sold to then provide a basis for rewarding farmers for their commitment to the Project with a financial incentive to supplement their income. Thus, AWD allows rice farmers to adapt to water scarcity and mitigates methane emissions in parallel. The Project represents the first stage of a nationwide program in which the next stage will be the UPRIIS irrigated system in Luzon.

The aim of the project is to facilitate the roll-out of conservation agriculture in regions of South Africa where it is not prevalent. The intention is to at a minimum, assist farmers to replace conventional cultivation practices with the three essential components of CA – no till, cultivating a variety of species and the maintenance of organic cover through the year. To facilitate the initial adoption as well as long-term maintenance of these essential components and potential additional activities, a broad set of activities are required that are centred around three themes or goals: 1. To address the lack of regionally specific awareness, knowledge, evidence and models. 2. To build regional technical support programmes and peer networks based on trust and evidence, and 3. To create an attractive financial incentive package to sustain implementation over the long-term. Agoro Carbon USA Cropland Program is a grouped VCS project implemented by Agoro Carbon Alliance. The program will implement a package of regenerative agricultural land management activities such as but not limited to reduced and zero tillage, cover cropping, improved nitrogen management as a means to reduce GHG and decarbonize agriculture. The implementation of these practices will lead to increases in carbon sequestration rates in the soil, reduced soil disturbance and soil erosion, improved crop residue and water management, as well as potentially reducing the total usage of fossil fuels. The main objective of the program is to provide the financial, agronomic and educational support needed for growers to adopt new farming practices that not only produce agricultural products in a sustainable and profitable way, but also have a positive impact on climate change.

Gujarat is one of the highest cotton producing states in India. Cotton is a fibre crop grown during monsoon season (locally called as kharif season) under irrigated conditions. Saurashtra region of Gujarat state contributes to the 70% of the total cotton production of the state. Although cotton is a major cash crop of Saurashtra region, but it is one of the highly water intensive crops of India. Cotton farming also requires high input of synthetic nitrogen chemical fertilizers. Nitrogenous fertilizers are one of major sources of nitrous oxide – a potent greenhouse gas with Global Warming Potential (GWP) of 298 – causing global climatic changes. In view of aforementioned problem statement, Greneity is proposing a grouped project in Saurashtra region of Gujarat for promotion of sustainable cotton farming which not only aims to addresses the associated environmental and climatic issues but also emphasizes on improvement of socio-economic conditions of the cotton growing farmers. Specifically, the project activity implemented reduction in synthetic nitrogen fertilizer application in agricultural practices as well as enhancing use of organic amendments like composts produced from agricultural residues and mulching of post-harvest residues. These agricultural practices can reduce the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions as well as remove atmospheric carbon dioxide into the soil organic carbon (SOC)

The aim of the climate protection project is to increase soil organic matter content in arable soils and simultaneously reduce agricultural greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions via a broad scale-up of regenerative agriculture. Therefore the project intends to motivate as many farmers as possible to convert from conventional farming, the most common type in Germany, to regenerative agriculture practices. This is done through financial support and in-depth knowledge transfer using digital platforms (company-owned web application & mobile application). Today, conventional agriculture is the predominant agricultural practice in Germany, with dramatic consequences for the overall soil fertility and the soil carbon stocks. Therefore, one focus of the project is to reduce CO2 by increasing the SOC stock. But at the same time the project considers the reduction of CO2, CH4 and N2O emissions from agricultural management activities, such as fossil fuel consumption, fertiliser use or livestock production. This enables a holistic view on the development of GHG-emissions related to regenerative management methods. Other positive side-effects of large scale project application can be taken into account, such as an overall improvement of the soil fertility and health including i) an increase in water storage capacity, thus providing a higher drought resilience, ii) an increase in anion retention capacity of the soils, thus reducing nitrate leaching rates to aquifers and iii) an improvement of the soil structural stability and infiltration rates, thus minimising the risk of soil erosion events. The project aims to be validated according to the Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management (VM0042).

The project plans to promote improved water management practices in rice cultivation instead of using the traditional practice of continuously flooded irrigation. AWD/DSR are proven methods to reduced methane emission by as much as 48% compared to flooded conditions where large amounts of methane (CH4) gets generated because of anaerobic decomposition. This project is predicted to generate important co-benefits of reducing water usage during rice cultivation, decrease pest and disease attacks, improve soil health etc. Further they're also beneficial for reduced cost of cultivation for small land holders

Agoro Carbon USA Pastureland Program is a grouped VCS project implemented by Agoro Carbon Alliance. The program will implement a package of regenerative land management activities in pasturelands, these include nutrient management, increasing species diversity, rotational grazing and other regenerative practices. The implementation of these practices will lead to an increase in carbon sequestration rates in the soil, increase in forage quality, overall animal and soil health and improved water management. The main objective of this program is to provide financial, agronomic and educational support to ranchers to implement the aforementioned practices. During the project lifetime, enrolled ranchers will be assisted by the Agoro Carbon agronomic team to implement improved agricultural management practices from their current system standard to a system that capitalizes on sustainable, regenerative production.

The Western Kenya Soil Carbon Project promotes the adoption of a range of Sustainable Agricultural Land Management technologies including reduced tillage, mulching, cover crops, green manure, composting, soil & water conservation, integrated pest management, and agroforestry on croplands and surrounding areas for watershed restoration and protection. It is implemented western Kenya in three counties: Bungoma, Kakamega and Siaya. Due to its more favourable agroecology, the region is densely populated, and the lands are extensively cultivated with limited natural vegetation. Farmers practice subsistence agriculture, characterized by low inputs, low yields, and continuous loss of soil fertility. The project is managed by Soil-Carbon Certification Services Ltd (SCCS), a non-for-profit company. SCCS is contracting implementation partner (IPs) to support farmers in their land restoration efforts. The project’s main goals are improved yields, food and incomes for farmers, increased resilience to climate change, and climate change mitigation via increased carbon sequestration in soils and plant biomass. The project activities will generate carbon credits that will be certified under the VCS program and monetized and invested in the project activities to ensure sustainability of the project goals. It is a grouped project covering 32,000 ha, with total VCUs 1.87 million tCO2. Participating smallholders are organized in farmer groups for efficient extension services delivery. The groups sign agreements to be project participants after due process of local stakeholders’ consultations and are then entitled to all extension services and support from the project. The group agreements oblige them to adopt and implement SALM technologies on their lands, support project monitoring, and transfer emission reduction units to the project. The project has a 20-year crediting period and applies the VCS Methodology VM0017 Adoption of Sustainable Agricultural Land Management, Version 1.0.

Sagri Co., Ltd is going to decrease the usage of Nitrogen Fertilizer in India and Thailand by using the soil detect technology by satellite images. Indian farmers are over-applying chemical fertilizers. However, the rising price of chemical fertilizers has put small-scale farmers' farming operations in a critical situation. In addition, excessive application of nitrogen fertilizers is bad for the environment for the following reasons. First, excessive nitrogen fertilizer applied to the ground causes excessive denitrification. In the process of denitrification, N₂O, a greenhouse gas with a greenhouse effect about 300 times greater than CO₂, is emitted. In addition, excessive application of synthetic nitrogen fertilizers can cause water pollution. Excess nitrogen that runs off into rivers and streams and enters people's bodies through drinking water and aquatic products poses a health hazard. Therefore, by applying the appropriate amount of nitrogen fertilizer to the soil, the amount of nitrogen fertilizer applied can be reduced, helping farmers to operate their farms, preventing global warming, and reducing health hazards to people. Sagri is engaged in the business of solving global issues related to agriculture and the environment by combining satellite data and AI machine learning technology, and is promoting its core technology, AI Polygon, which uses image technology with AI to analyze high-resolution satellite data and automatically plot farmland in Japan and overseas. Sagri is also developing a technology to analyze soil chemical indices on farmland after plowing, using wavelength data obtained from satellite data and AI-based machine learning.In this project, Sagri will use this technology to analyze soil chemical indices to determine the appropriate amount of fertilizer to be applied, and will receive carbon credits for encouraging farmers to use variable fertilizer application.

The project activity is an 'Alternate wetting and drying (AWD)' activity that is a water saving strategy in irrigated rice production. The main objective of the project is to switch from continuously flooded rice fields to fields that alternately encompass flooded and non-flooded phases which can save significant amount of irrigation water. Thus, the project activity has been designed to change from continuously flooded to intermittent flooded condition during rice cultivation which is conducted in different blocks in the district of Bhopal, Hoshangabad, Raisen and Sehore of the state of Madhya Pradesh, in India. A total of 8,085 hectare for single-cropping rice has been covered under the project activity. During rice cultivation, controllable irrigation and drainage according to rice growth requirements can save water resources, and also at the same time will also reduce methane emission from soil organic matter under anaerobic conditions (in the flooded state). Additionally, in the project activity compost will be used for soil application in the rice fields and thus replace the application of synthetic nitrogen fertilizer. It is estimated that about 58,722 tCO2e emission reductions will be generated annually across the crediting period.

The High Impact Carbon Farming Program of Lithuania is promoted, financed, and implemented by UAB Heavy Finance. “UAB Heavy Finance” main activity is providing crowdfunded loans to farmers for equipment purchases, cash flow, or other farming activities. The Sustainability department of UAB Heavy Finance is in charge of GHG project design and implementation. The project aims to promote Improved Agricultural Land Management (IALM) practices for reducing GHGs. The practices for CO2 sequestration are the following- reduced soil disturbance, tailored fertiliser management, improved (plant) residue management and cover cropping, and improved crop rotation and harvesting.

The project “NaturAll Carbon Program – Conservation Agriculture and Land Management in Brazil” belongs to NaturAll Carbon Limited and is located in Brazil, South America. The area is located in 23 states, covering a total area of 414.8 million hectares. The extension of the project covers four Brazilian biomes, Caatinga, Cerrado, Atlantic Forest and Pampa. It is very important to highlight that in order to preserve forests and swamps, lands from Amazon and Pantanal biomes will not be part of this project. As the leading causes of high GHG emissions and agricultural soil degradation have already been identified and are linked to inadequate management practices. But, although there are several studies and research data from all over Brazil, until now, there has been no efficient program to raise awareness and support rural producers in the transition to conservationist soil management on their agricultural property. Adopting conservation practices in the areas of agricultural and livestock activities, the goal will be to help reduce and remove GHG from the atmosphere, increase Soil Organic Carbon (SOC), avoid soil degradation (physical, chemical, and biological), improving soil fertility and productivity, creating a better resilience to extreme weather events, providing food security and preserving natural resources and their ecosystem services. The choice of instances inserted in the project will be based on implementing one or more regenerative or conservationist practices from November 1st, 2019, which are not common in the region, and there is additionality. The project intends to expand over time and reach multiple instances, and a range of agriculture and livestock activities in the four Brazilian biomes described previously to help drive resilient and sustainable agropastoral systems in these locations.

The “Olive Groves for Carbon Farming” Project consists in new super-high-density organic trees crop plantations in Centre and South of Italy for olive cultivation with the implementation of innovative precision organic agriculture practices as Climate Change adaptation and mitigation Natural Based Project. The Project activities take place in several Italian farms of Central and Southern Regions which are located in the Mediterranean Climate Area. Since “The Mediterranean region is a hotspot for highly interconnected climate risks” (IPCC 2021) and for this area it is expected a faster warming with respect to global temperature average rise (UN environment program 2020), The Project builds new resilient crops contributing to the climate mitigation through carbon reduction and removal, securing in the long-term food production and cultural identity. The Project consists of crop change on agricultural land, from annual crops to perennial organic tree plantations with a super-high-density of 1,200/1,600 olive trees per hectare, with respect to traditional olive groves density of less 200 trees per hectare. The Project involves changes and improvements of traditional and local common agriculture practices as: improved water management with new water dripline irrigation system, tillage reduction, fertilizer reduction, cover crops implementation like green manures and precision farming by vegetation monitoring with satellites and drones. The Project started in 2019 in some farms, it was then implemented in others and its accomplishment is expected for all the remaining farms by 2025 for a total estimated area of around 2,500 hectares.

This project aims to help farmers deploy improved cropland management and regenerative agricultural practices in the croplands of Kenya. Over time, these croplands have undergone severe degradation due to anthropological factors, environmental conditions, and recurring natural calamities. Around 75% of the population of Kenya is dependent on agriculture, and the sector supports a majority of the country’s food requirements. However, since agricultural production is largely rain-fed and around 80% of Kenya’s geography comprises arid and semi-arid regions, the occurrence of erratic rains and frequent droughts has imposed constraints on its productivity and stability. In addition to natural disasters like droughts, degradation of land is greatly accelerated by unsustainable land use and management practices. Furthermore, in several parts of the country, soils are deficient in nitrogen, phosphorous and potassium, thereby resulting in poor vegetation cover. In this context, the opportunity to introduce improved cropland management practices will significantly help the croplands of the region and restore soil organic matter to their land, creating carbon removals while improving overall soil health. The project activities include the adopt of practices such as no-till or reduced tilling, mulching with crop residues, reduced synthetic fertilizer application, using organic manures, water management, improved crop planting and harvesting methods, and agroforestry activities. These practices are proven ways to increase soil organic carbon, preventing further degradation of croplands and their soils, and enabling farmers to improve their productivity.

Flooding conditions in rice fields emit the most CH4, while intermittently flooded rice fields create a high quantity of N2O. Emissions of GHGs from rice fields can be reduced by modifying irrigation patterns, regulating organic additives, and using suitable rate and quantity of Nitrogen fertilizer. Irrigation practice such as Alternate wetting and drying (AWD) method has been observed to reduce GHG emissions in comparison to the traditional method of flooding. The time intervals between dry and wet conditions help in the transition from aerobic to anaerobic soil conditions, thus alternate wetting, and drying method leads in a significant reduction in methane generation1. Thus, the project employs AWD method to reduce the CH4 emissions. This will also lead to reduction in the water consumption, thus decreasing the input cost of the farmer. Before implementation of the project activity, the farmers were following the traditional flooding method, leading to the emissions of methane in the atmosphere. The project proponent conducted training programs and meeting with the farmers to make them aware about the benefits of adopting AWD, followed by the distribution and installation of AWD pipe in the fields of enrolled farmers. The first instance of the project is located in Haryana state covering an area of 4973 hectares. Furthermore, as it is a grouped project, the project activity will be implemented in other rice growing states of India in the future instances. Annual average emissions from the project are 48,853 tCO2eq.

La Gioia farm is located in La Gioia, Alessandria in Northern Italy. The coordinates are attached as a KML file. Several agricultural practices will be implemented or modified on the land. Taken together, the goal is to reduce the carbon emissions currently emitted by this farm and raise the carbon stored in the soil. In addition, the selected measures will contribute to improving crop yields and soil health. To do so, the following methods will be applied on site; Reduction of the inorganic fertilizer application, change of irrigation system, Incorporation of crops residues into the soil, Tillage reduction, Cover crop implementation, Reduction of the fossil fuel use, Switch from crops to woody biomass The sectoral scope 14 – Agriculture Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU) is applicable to the project. Within this sector, this project has been developed under the scope of the methodology for improved agricultural land management (VM0042 VCS methodology). The project has been found eligible under the scope of the VCS program as it meets all requirements established by the program. The crediting period chosen for this project is of 25 years, renewable 4 times. The period lasts from the 01/06/22 to the 1/6/2047. We estimated that 211,7 tCO2/year will be stored in the soil or not emitted.

The High Impact Carbon Farming Program of Poland is a joint initiative between UAB Heavy Finance (HF) and farmers within the Poland Republic borders. The program utilizes private capital to implement, and adopt improved agricultural land management for a long-term period, thus changing the mindset and establishing climate change mitigation and biodiversity-friendly practices.

The regenerative livestock farming carbon project in Colombia is developed by the project developers Sosty S.A.S and Carbono Local+ GmbH. The project titled “Regenerative Livestock Carbon Project with a Participatory Approach in Colombia” is a comprehensive initiative developed by the project developers encompassing a variety of activities aimed at improving grazing practices, restoring soil health, and enhancing the resilience and well-being of farmers. The primary objectives of the project are to reduce overall emissions through carbon sequestration in the soil while simultaneously improving farm productivity and conserving biodiversity in grazing areas. These goals will be achieved by enhancing livestock production practices, specifically by ceasing grassland burning and implementing adaptive multi-paddock grazing. The project will also promote the diversity of forages rather than the monoculture of pastures. This includes the management of native savannahs and introduced pastures, incorporating nitrogen-fixing species, and integrating silvo pastoral systems. The grouped project is developed within the Colombian agricultural frontier (located in five different eco-regions), which is the delimited area defined by the government, where livestock husbandry and agricultural activities are allowed to be developed. The project’s start date is 20.01.2020 and its crediting period goes on to 40 years. It targets a total 250,000 ha that can generate an annual average and total GHG emission reductions and removals of 292,050 tCO2eq per year and a total of 11,802,000 tCO2eq of emission reductions by 2060.

Since December 2019, Shangani Ranch has adopted land management practices aimed at reversing the steady degradation of land due to selective grazing practices. To achieve this, the ranch adopted Holistic Planned Grazing (HPG). The Shangani ranch HPG carbon project aims to remove greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions via enhancing soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration through improved grazing management. The project area of 65,000 ha is located in Shangani, Matebeleland South province of Zimbabwe (19.75oS, 29.40oE). This area is split into 45,000 ha of Shangani ranch to the north and 20,000 ha of an area referred to as Shangani Headquarters (HQ) to the south. The project aims to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by sequestering soil organic carbon (SOC). The improved SOC sequestration will be driven by an improved rotational grazing system, referred to as HPG, which emphasizes high intensity short duration grazing and has the potential to reduce land degradation due to overgrazing by allowing grassland time to recover. Overgrazing has been cited as one of the main drivers accelerating soil degradation and loss, leading to poor landscape stability, water quality and ecosystem functioning. The predominant land-use has been low-level game hunting, wildlife conservation and rotational cattle grazing in designated paddocks. The Shangani ranch management moved away from rotational cattle grazing to a Holistic Planned GrazingTM (HPG) programme in December 2019.

The “carbono rural AR NEA” project aims to support sustainable grazing practices in Northeastern Argentina (NEA). The project will target farmers that apply unsustainable grazing practices in NEA grasslands/pasturelands and encourage their transition to better grazing practices. These changes are expected to improve the productivity and sustainability of grazing systems while enhancing soil organic carbon sequestration and reducing GHG emissions.

Helping farmers transition to zero-input, high-output farms with happy cows and thriving ecosystems. The ruumi grazing app has been developed by farmers, software engineers, and data scientists to help overcome the challenges of implementing managed grazing. It uses a combination of satellite data, soil maps, seed-mix data, and state-of-the-art machine learning techniques to provide farmers with real-time information—and the user-friendly tools they need to manage their livestock with confidence. By helping farmers manage their land, ruumi collects the information necessary to create carbon credits of the highest quality. This gives farmers access to a new revenue stream, which goes directly into financing the transition to more sustainable practices. The data from ruumi’s platform combined with satellite imagery provides carbon credit buyers with unique, real-time insights into how their investment is helping create a better world. Carbon credits not only measure the increase in soil organic matter, but also consider how this increase has come to pass. Emissions from fertilizers, fuel usage, and methane emissions are taken into account, and only long-lived net improvements are certified. ruumi was founded to help farmers transition to zero-input, high-output farms with happy cows and thriving ecosystems. Its mission is to make farmers profitable without subsidies, get companies excited about removing their greenhouse gases from the atmosphere, and reconnect consumers with the people and places that produce their food.

The Involtor Future Agriculture East-Europe is a grouped project gathering under the same program major agricultural areas from Romania and aiming at the scientific implementation of modern agricultural practices that helps preserve the Planet's climate, increase the resilience of agriculture and food security to climate change. The project provides a wide range of support for farmers, aiming for a safe transition to regenerative agriculture by implementing effective practices that sequester carbon in the soil, reduce / remove the emissions of CH4, N2O, CO2 that agriculture emits today in significant quantities, and in exchange for the performance monitored by this Project, farmers will receive income from verified carbon credits. The project pursues the implementation of 8 of UN SDG’s seeking certification with VERRA's SD ViSta - Verified Impact Standard. The initial phase of Project considers 1st of December 2019 as the baseline date in which the first agricultural practices implementation started.

The project intends to include producers dedicated to extensive agriculture (corn, soybeans, wheat, sunflower, cotton, and other crops), and extensive cattle ranching, mostly cattle and grazing grasslands, pastures, agropastoral, and silvo-pastoral. Given the characteristics of the country, farm and ranch production dates from no more than 200 years ago. During most of the 20th century, the farms were managed in a rather extensive manner and with aggressive tillage systems, which caused widespread declines in the organic matter content of the soils. This lasted until the end of that century, when for different reasons the producers adopted zero tillage systems, which are what predominate today (more than 90%). The projects to be implemented are expected to mitigate climate change both by reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and by capturing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) and storing it as stable carbon in the soil, which must be recarbonized. The greatest efforts to reduce GHG emissions will be due to the adoption of better nitrogen fertilization technologies, which include alternative sources of nitrogen and variable rate fertilization that reduce nitrous oxide (N2) emissions from fertilized soils, the intensification of agricultural rotations with greater incorporation of winter crops, nitrogen fixing species and cover crops, and improved grazing management in livestock, which increase carbon stocks and with improvements in digestibility that reduce methane (CH4) emissions due to enteric fermentation. It is estimated that with these improvements, which are not currently widespread even among producers, it will be possible to reduce between 0.5 and 3 tons of CO2e/ha/year. Obviously, the total amount will depend on the area committed by the producers. This area is expected to reach more than 160 thousand hectares. If this is so, it is expected to mitigate almost 2 million tons CO2e at the end of this project.

The project activity promotes sustainable agriculture practices among cotton farmers in order to reduce the usage of synthetic fertilizer and biomass burning. The project activity aims to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from the agricultural fields which mainly source from the stubble burning, excess use of fertilizer and as a result excess water requirement for irrigation etc

The AgreenaCarbon Project aims to reduce agricultural GHG emissions through the implementation of activities that are central principles of regenerative agriculture. The Project intends to help farmers transition to regenerative agriculture by applying sustainable agricultural land management practices (ALM) in order to maintain yields while ensuring long-term viability of their farms and land. Regenerative agriculture describes holistic farming practices that improve the soil fertility and enhance the storage of soil organic carbon (SOC) and ‘focuses on the regeneration of living soil, improved micro hydrology, and conserving biodiversity at all levels while enhancing inputs use-efficiency and ecosystem system services.’ The AgreenaCarbon Project assists farmers in the transition from conventional, intensive farming practices to ones that avoid soil disturbances and increase the amount of organic soil amendments all while reducing the use of synthetic fertilisers. The focal point of these practices is reducing tillage to reduce soil disturbance with the addition of the other activities as a combined suite of activities that contribute to soil fertility. The Project facilitates the transition through a carbon payment programme which provides economic incentives to change existing agricultural practices, described as project activities. The programme is located across Europe and is based in temperate climates.

Il progetto riguarda la riduzione delle emissioni di CO2 derivanti dal mancato consumo di fitofarmaci e la riduzione dell'irrigazione su 8.512 ettari di grano nelle regioni PUGLIA, BASILICATA, e CALABRIA

Rice is the country's most significant agricultural product; it is grown on 43.86 million hectares in India and contributes to more than 20% of world rice output (158.2 Tg in 2013). Rice is farmed in practically every state in India, and its production is directly related to the country's food security. Additionally, it is a significant source of income and employment. Rice production, on the other hand, is a substantial source of critical and long-lasting GHGs such as CH 4 and N 2 O, posing a huge threat to sustainable agriculture. Rice fields provide approximately 30% and 11% of total agricultural CH 4 and N 2 O emissions, respectively. According to early US-EPA study, paddy in India produced around 37.8 Tg CH 4 per year. GHG emissions from rice fields may be minimized by changing irrigation patterns, managing organic additions, and utilizing the appropriate rate and amount of nitrogen fertilizer. Irrigation practices such as alternate wetting and drying (AWD) have been shown to lower GHG emissions when compared to typical flooding methods. The time intervals between dry and wet circumstances aid in the shift from aerobic to anaerobic soil conditions, resulting in a considerable reduction in methane output. As a result, the project adopts the AWD approach to minimize CH 4 emissions. This will also result in a reduction in water use, lowering the farmer's input costs. Prior to the execution of the project activity, the farmers used the traditional flooding approach, which resulted in methane emissions into the atmosphere. The project proponent along with local implementation partner held training sessions and meetings with farmers to educate them on the benefits of using AWD, which was followed by the distribution and installation of AWD pipe in the fields of registered farmers. Location: The first instance of the project is located in Madhya Pradesh (Hoshangabad, Raisen, Sehore and Bhopal districts). The annual average emissions is 53,369 tCO 2 eq.

This project will support the transition of 11,000 ha towards Regenerative Agriculture in Brittany, France with C.100 farmers. The farming model thrilling soil health is called conservation agriculture and has locally bee n proof tested for 20 years by an innovative group of pioneer farmers and Livelihoods Venture is willing to scale up to local farmers, including young settlers, with the support of local public authorities. The farming model is called conservation agriculture because it conserves and restores soil organic matter by protecting the soil micro and macro organism habitats. It builds on three main practices: permanent soil cover, diversified rotations and low soil disturbance Therefore, this project is expecting to generate GHG emission reductions and removals mostly through soil organic carbon storage. Conventional agriculture in Brittany is the most common scenario existing on local farms, prior to the implementation of the project. Be tween two main cash crops cycles, land is not producing and soil remains uncovered for weeks, increasing risks of run off and topsoil erosion. Those risks are amplified by the common use of tillage, as the main “soil preparation” practice. By implementing this project, we estimate a total GHC emission reductions and removals of C.370, 000 t CO2e over a 20 year period To estimate the carbon potential of the project, we designed a set of assumptions embedding agronomic specifications, recruitment pace, and the success rate of farmers’ practices adoption. To assess the carbon inputs, we have set a range of 10 typical baseline rotations and 10 regenerative agriculture rotations that we have combined with 3 soil types, till age, low tillage and no tillage options. Carbon pools generating credits is the increase of carbon soil stocks (91%), the reduction of fuel consumptions (5%), the decrease of nitrogen fertilizer upstream (3%) and nitrogen field impact (1%).

Paddy fields are the most dominant anthropogenic sources of methane to the atmosphere (5-20% of the total emission from all anthropogenic sources ). Anaerobic decomposition of organic material in flooded rice fields produces methane, which escapes to the atmosphere primarily by transport through the rice plants. The annual amount of CH4 emitted from a given area of rice is a function of the number and duration of crops grown, water regimes before and during the cultivation period, and organic and inorganic soil amendments. Soil type, temperature, and rice cultivar also affect CH4 emissions. This CH4 emission-intensive cultivation method will be targeted by the proposed programme, that will involve the implementation of the technology/measures that result in reduced anaerobic decomposition of organic matter in rice cropping soils and thus reduced generation of methane. The project activity comprises of grouped projects of rice fields implementing the following methods: (a) Rice farms that change the water regime during the cultivation period from continuously to intermittent flooded conditions and/or a shortened period of flooded conditions; (b) Alternate wetting and drying method (AWD) (c) Rice farms that change their rice cultivation practice from transplanted to direct-seeded rice (DSR). Thus, the measure will consist of AWD and/or DSR in combination with adjusted water management system in rice cultivation. The Project Activity Instances will be implemented in Kamareddy district in the state of Telangana. Each instance will be of 5000 Hectares will be implemented in Kamareddy, Telangana State.

The annual amount of CH4 emitted from a given area of rice is a function of the number and duration of crops grown, water regimes before and during the cultivation period, and organic and inorganic soil amendments.
