This CH4 emission-intensive cultivation method will be targeted by the proposed programme, that will involve the implementation of the technology/measures that result in reduced anaerobic decomposition of organic matter in rice cropping soils and thus reduced generation of methane. The project activity comprises of grouped projects of rice fields implementing the following methods: (a) Rice farms that change the water regime during the cultivation period from continuously to intermittent flooded conditions and/or a shortened period of flooded conditions; (b) Alternate wetting and drying method (AWD) (c) Rice farms that change their rice cultivation practice from transplanted to direct-seeded rice (DSR). Thus, the measure will consist of AWD and/or DSR in combination with an adjusted water management system in rice cultivation. The Project Activity Instances will be implemented in the Mahabubabad district in Telangana. Each instance of 5000 Hectares will be implemented in Mahabubabad, Telangana State.

The High Impact Soil Carbon Program of Lithuania is a joint initiative between UAB Heavy Finance (HF) farmers within the Lithuanian Republic borders. The program utilizes private capital to implement, and adopt improved agricultural land management for a long-term period, thus changing the mindset and establishing climate change mitigation and biodiversity-friendly practices. It is a first-of-its-kind program in Lithuania and the Baltics. It aims to assist farmers in overcoming barriers that prevent adopting sustainable land management practices by providing scientific knowledge, training, and technical and financial support to adopt mitigating climate activities successfully. The program is designed to expand over time and cover a range of conservational farming practices in Lithuania to help drive the change from the current conventional agriculture toward resilient and sustainable agrifood systems.

The Carbon Farming Program of Lithuania is a joint initiative between UAB Heavy Finance (HF) and farmers within the Lithuanian Republic borders. The program utilizes private capital to implement and adopt improved agricultural land management long-term, thus changing the mindset and establishing climate change mitigation and biodiversity-friendly practices. The Program aims to reward farmers for the positive results of fostering improved agricultural land management practices by sharing the revenue obtained from the sale of VCUs generated through the verified greenhouse gas emissions reductions and removals projects. Project activities are helping farmers to reach the balance in the triple bottom line - economic, environmental, and social. Improved agriculture land management refers to the techniques that focus on soil health and fertility by storing and increasing organic carbon, reducing anthropogenic gasses from excessive use of chemical fertilizers in the context of the offered program, accelerating changes to pre-existing agricultural management practices, and adopting regenerative methods.

The proposed VCS Agricultural Land Management project activity aims to implement organic farming to reduce the greenhouse gases emission of Carbon dioxide, Methane, and Nitrous oxide through enhancing soil carbon pool, reducing use of chemical fertilizer, making compost out of biomass residue, and fuel saving through lesser consumption of agricultural machineries. Along with the reduction of greenhouse gases, the project also aims to increase the capacity of soil to sequester carbon and enhance nutrients by mulching through organic material, and assimilation of compost and vermicomposting manure. Prior to the project implementation –The farmers in the proposed project were managing their farmlands and agriculture using conventional farming which was causing high GHG emission. The project started on 17 June 2020 in the Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh state of India. The project is estimated to reduce emission by 57127 tCO2/annum and total 5,71,272 tCO2 throughout its crediting period of 10 years

The Bayer Agricultural Carbon Program enables the adoption of regenerative agricultural practices on continental United States row crop land through financial incentives and technical support. Participants in the Project are individual farmers and field managers who have implemented one or more practice changes on their farm that will increase the deposition of soil organic carbon, reduce nitrogen fertilizer losses in the form of N2O, or reduce on-farm energy consumption.

The Anew Agri-Carbon Project Aggregation 1 enables the adoption of regenerative agricultural practices on continental United States row crop land through financial incentives and technical support. Participants in the Project are individual farmers and field managers who have implemented one or more practice changes on their farm that will increase the deposition of soil organic carbon, reduce nitrogen fertilizer losses in the form of N 2 O, or reduce on farm energy consumption.

The project involves the implementation of sustainable agriculture practices in wheat and maize cultivation in India. Sustainable agriculture practices can help to ensure that this vital sector remains productive, resilient, and profitable for farmers, while also protecting natural resources and preserving the environment. Conservation agriculture is a sustainable agriculture system that involves three key principles: minimizing soil disturbance, maintaining soil cover, and practicing crop rotation. This system is designed to protect the soil and improve its health, which in turn helps to increase crop productivity and reduce environmental damage. Along with that balanced nutrient management with optimum nitrogen application is also considered as a climate friendly agriculture practice. The project is designed as a grouped project which will be implemented in the states of India. The first instance of the project will be implemented in Bihar, Haryana, Punjab and West Bengal in a total area of 100,000 ha of wheat and maize cultivating fields.

The objective of the proposed VCS Sustainable Agricultural Land Management (SALM) project activity aims to transition the farmers into practicing more sustainable cultivation practices in sugarcane production. The SALM project is expected to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions or increase sequestration of carbon in soil and biomass.These sustainable practices will improve the soils of the farmers and enhance their resilience to climate change

The AFOLU Carbon project focuses on reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from cotton cultivation through a variety of measures and technologies The project will engage with medium, small and marginal farmers and promote managing the use of synthetic fertilizers, reduce the use of fossil fuels in cotton cultivation by promoting more efficient ways for irrigation and encourage the implementation of agroforestry practices.

A large percentage of the total populations in India draw income from the agriculture. These populations reside in the rural area commonly addressed as farmers were performing the conventional farming i.e., use of fertilizers, use of synthetic fertilizers, using machinery’s for tillage, and residue burning across the year which would result in emissions all the year round. In this proposed project the PP intends to promote activities organic and/or natural farming where farmers are encouraged to produce the manures in their farm land, control pest infestation using natural ingredients, practice low or no tillage, avoid or stop residue burning, enhance the soil organic carbon & sequestration, and establish market for premium price covering 6500.00 ha of cropland in Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Goa and Karnataka in states of India. Several research in the past (Jarvan et all., 2017 and Chahal et all., 2020) shows that such practices are boon for the farmers as well for the environment.

The proposed project activity will mobilize resource-poor private smallholders, forest dwellers and forest dependent communities to practice agroforestry, horticulture, plantation crops etc on degraded farm lands and forest lands assigned to tribals under the Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006. As these lands are currently under subsistence agriculture, various environment friendly technology based agroforestry and horticulture practices, Climate Smart Agriculture (CSA) and Natural Climate Solutions (NCS) will be promoted for sustainable land management, to help improve their livelihoods and also to aid climate change adaptation & mitigation. The project is located in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh. It aims to link those resource poor landholders/forest dependent people with voluntary carbon markets, in order to optimize the land use and generate Emission Reductions (ERs), from quantifying Above Ground Biomass (AGB), Below Ground Biomass (BGB) and Soil Organic Carbon (SOC). The Emission Reductions through the project activity will be measured, quantified and verified with reference to a baseline through representative sampling. In the absence of the project, the lands would have remained degraded, as the resource poor private farmers, tribals and communities would continue practicing subsistence agriculture. The project implements reforestation on 2000 ha of degraded forest/farm lands and will be later scaled up to 20,000 ha over a period of 5 years. The reforestation activities under the project were initiated in 2020. The project is estimated to generate 1,05,600 credits/year on average over a period of 20 years.

The project aims to promote sustainable agriculture practices among maize farmers and mitigate greenhouse gas emissions through the use of carbon finance mechanisms. The project will work with maize farmers in Belagavi to adopt sustainable farming practices, including the reduction of fertilizers and pesticides, crop mixing, and improving soil health. These practices will help reduce greenhouse gas emissions and improve the quality of soil, leading to increased crop yields and enhanced livelihoods for farmers.

The sustainable farming project aims to implement various technologies and measures to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and enhance carbon sequestration. The project seeks to promote sustainable agricultural practices, including the adoption of conservation agriculture, agroforestry, and efficient use of water and energy.

The proposed Crop Residue Management project developed by the Godrej Properties Ltd. (GPL) is implementing across 15 villages of Gurdaspur, Punjab by the Feedback Foundation Charitable Trust (FFCT). The project aims at developing a unique soil carbon sequestration project with an objective of addressing the severe crop residue burning -air pollution issue, in an environmentally sustainable and cost-effective manner. The project integrates the adoption of SALM practices, as a permanent solution to stubble burning and is estimated to be carried out in 4015.01 hectares of croplands that are located in the villages of Sri Hargobindpur Block namely, Sakala, Bolewal, Yeel Bajju, Cheema Kalan, Mike, Talwandi Bhinder, Mandiala, Athwal, Ladda Munda, Nangal, Momanwal, Sandhwan, Pandori, Attepur, and Kisankot.

The Carbon Credit project in Morocco initiated by Innovx proposes regenerative agricultural practices, focusing on conservation agriculture and crop nutrient stewardship. It aims to enhance agricultural soil health in six regions: Rabat-Salé-Kenitra, Beni Mellal-Khenifra, Marrakech-Safi, Tangier-Tetouan-Al Hoceima, Fes-Meknes (including the provinces of Fes, Meknes, Taounate, El Hajeb, Moulay Yacoub, Sefrou), and Casablanca-Settat (including the provinces of Casablanca, Settat, Berrechid, Benslimane, El Jaddida). The initiative covers 750,000 hectares, starting with 50,000 hectares in the first year and expanding annually. The project targets application of regenerative agriculture at scale with the help of Employing Sustainable Agricultural Land Management (SALM) technology including conservation agriculture and reduced application of nitrogen, that results in increased crop yields, food security, diversified farmer income, and climate change mitigation through elevated soil carbon and plant biomass. The Project is aligned with the Moroccan Ministry's goal to transition one million hectares to Zero-tillage by 2030, the project operates with a 10-year crediting period under the VCS-approved Methodology VM0017. Estimated annual average Emission Reductions (ER) reach 1402165, totalling 14021652 over the project duration. This initiative integrates environmental conservation, socio-economic development, and sustainable agriculture in Morocco's specified regions.

In the proposed project area, the farmers were practicing conventional farming methods viz., the use of artificial fertilizers, using heavy machinery for the tillage, and residue burning across the year which would result in emissions. The project focuses on promoting eco-friendly activities such as organic and/or natural farming where farmers are encouraged to produce the manures in their farmland, control pest infestation using natural ingredients, practice low or no tillage, avoid or stop residue burning, enhance the soil organic carbon & sequestration, and agro-forestry. Further, the project focuses on supporting the farmer's community, to pursue the best & sustainable agricultural practices, and strengthen the socio-economics of the participating farmers, such as distribution of rain cover, drums, agri-equipments, blankets, plants distribution, providing financial support to set up vermicompost, educational materials, setting up computer education, medical check, first aid kits, and in future, the project would like to focus on Market linkage of the produce of farmers, Branding & marketing of wheat & wheat flour, and Branding & supply of cornflour. The project aims to reduce and sequester carbon leading to estimated GHG emission reductions or removals (tCO2e) of 113,600.00 tCO2e / year and the emissions reduction or removals by approximately 4,544,000 (four million five hundred forty-four thousand) tCO2e over the lifetime of the project.

The Transformational Regenerative Integrated Biodiverse Agriculture for Livelihoods (TRIBAL) Project is a landscape approach that aims to make it viable for small and marginal farmers to live off their land in a sustainable and profitable manner. The project will promote agroforestry and sustainable farming practices across within the Araku Valley in Vishakhapatnam District, Andhra Pradesh, India. Planned agroforestry and sustainable farming practices that will be promoted by the project include agroforestry utilizing both fruit and multi-purpose tree species, shade coffee systems, intercropping of pulses and millets, green manuring, mulching and organic composting. These activities will improve the livelihoods and well-being of the tribal landowners by achieving multiple objectives such as improved soil fertility, increased revenue generation, food security, reduced drudgery for women and increased biodiversity. Through this positive impact on climate, communities, and biodiversity the TRIBAL project aims to achieve both VCS and CCB Gold certification. This grouped project is being initiated in Paderu and Pedabayalu Mandals of Paderu Division in Vishakhapatnam District, with the intention of expanding to up to 11 Mandals within the Araku Valley landscape in future. The tribal people of this region were traditionally hunters and gatherers, relying on the forest for sustenance. The practice of shifting cultivation came in at the turn of the century. As the- forest began to get depleted, the tribal communities gradually become engaged in agriculture. Now, subsistence agriculture is the primary livelihood for nearly 99% of the tribes within the project region, with over 80% of the landholdings being less than one hectare in size.

The project aims to introduce sustainable agriculture practices like zero tillage, nutrient management, and reduction of nitrogen application with nutrient stewardship, in potato cultivation. Sustainable agriculture practices in potato cultivation in India can help to reduce greenhouse gas (GHGs) emissions and contribute to mitigating climate change. Zero tillage or reduced tillage practices can help to conserve soil moisture, reduce soil erosion, and improve soil health. By minimizing soil disturbance, zero tillage can also help to retain soil carbon, reducing carbon emissions and sequestering carbon in the soil. Balanced fertilization and the use of organic fertilizers, can help to reduce nitrogen loss and minimize nitrous oxide emissions with improved nutrient use efficiencies. By optimizing nitrogen application rates, farmers can also improve potato yield and quality The project is designed as a grouped project which will be implemented in the states of India.

The SALM project in Bangladesh aims to address the negative impacts of conventional farming practices on the environment, particularly greenhouse gas emissions. The project includes a range of measures and technologies designed to reduce emissions by promoting regenerative and sustainable farming practices.The activities include efficient use of irrigation water, mulching, reduction of chemical fertilizer and pesticide use through the use of organic amendments, applying green manure, and alternative pest control methods, avoidance of crop residue burning, and minimum tillage.

The project intends to include producers dedicated to extensive agriculture (corn, soybeans, wheat, sunflower, cotton, and other crops), and extensive cattle ranching, mostly cattle and grazing grasslands, pastures, agropastoral, and silvo-pastoral. Given the characteristics of the country, farm and ranch production dates from no more than 200 years ago. During most of the 20th century, the farms were managed in a rather extensive manner and with aggressive tillage systems, which caused widespread declines in the organic matter content of the soils. This lasted until the end of that century, when for different reasons the producers adopted zero tillage systems, which are what predominate today (more than 90%). The projects to be implemented are expected to mitigate climate change both by reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and by capturing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) and storing it as stable carbon in the soil, which must be recarbonized. The greatest efforts to reduce GHG emissions will be due to the adoption of better nitrogen fertilization technologies, which include alternative sources of nitrogen and variable rate fertilization that reduce nitrous oxide (N2) emissions from fertilized soils, the intensification of agricultural rotations with greater incorporation of winter crops, nitrogen fixing species and cover crops, and improved grazing management in livestock, which increase carbon stocks and with improvements in digestibility that reduce methane (CH4) emissions due to enteric fermentation. It is estimated that with these improvements, which are not currently widespread even among producers, it will be possible to reduce between 0.5 and 3 tons of CO2e/ha/year. Obviously, the total amount will depend on the area committed by the producers. This area is expected to reach more than 160 thousand hectares. If this is so, it is expected to mitigate almost 2 million tons CO2e at the end of this project.

The project activity based in Uganda intends to create a distinctive soil carbon (SOC) sequestration initiative with the goal of tackling the serious sugarcane crop residue burning air pollution and high synthetic fertilizer usage in a financially feasible and environmentally sustainable way.

In Bulgaria, the High Impact Carbon Farming Program is a joint project between UAB Heavy Finance and local farmers. This program aims to promote sustainable land management practices that help mitigate climate change and preserve biodiversity. It offers scientific knowledge, training, and financial and technical assistance to farmers, enabling them to overcome obstacles and adopt eco-friendly agricultural practices. The program's ultimate objective is to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by over 1 million tonnes during the project's duration.

The Regenerate Outcomes Farming Project supports British farms to transition away from intensive ‘conventional’ modes of food production and towards regenerative production systems via a tailored mentoring programme. The participating farms in this project implement several regenerative land management activities which reduce and remove GHG emissions. The farm types range from permanent pasture to lowland mixed and arable. The mentoring is based on the following regenerative principles: limit mechanical, chemical and physical disturbance of the soil; maintain the cover of plant residues on the soil surface; promote biodiversity and diversity of farming activity; keep living roots in the ground; and further integrate livestock into crop rotations. The project monitors changes to farm emissions and soil carbon stocks under a model and measure quantification approach which is regulated under VM0042.

Globally, agriculture generated nearly 9.3 billion tons of CO2 equivalent (CO2eq) emissions in 2018, considering emissions at the farm gate and related to land use/land use change. The major contributors to these emissions are methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) from farming activities. Projections suggest that by 2030, these emissions will increase by 15% compared to 2010 levels, reaching an annual total of nearly 7 billion tons. Varaha initiated a project to harness the substantial carbon sequestration and ecological rehabilitation potential of regenerative agriculture practices in the districts of Gujarat. The ongoing project aims to promote these practices among farms engaged in cultivating cotton, cotton-wheat, rice, legumes, maize-wheat and rice-wheat cropping system. The project aims to expedite the adoption of improved agricultural practices among Indian farmers. The project will be a grouped project, with new project activities, are being added over the lifespan of the project. The cotton-wheat/cotton cropping systems will be considered in the first instance of the project. For further instances, cotton, cotton-wheat, sugarcane, rice, legumes, maize-wheat and rice-wheat cropping system or crops will be considered. The project interventions or activities will be implemented in partnership with Aga Khan rural support program (India)-AKRSP (I). The project interventions were implemented in the year 2020. Starting with 25 thousand hectares, the area will be stabilized at 312,000 hectares in 2029 and maintained until 2040.

Currently, regenerative agriculture arises as a promising strategy to address the issues of food security and climate change. It embodies a comprehensive approach to farming that prioritizes the revitalization and enhancement of soil health, biodiversity, and ecosystem services. Through the adoption of regenerative practices, farmers have the potential to enhance both the productivity and profitability of their farms, while also playing a vital role in fostering a sustainable and resilient agricultural system that tackles the pressing challenges of our era. Varaha initiated a project to harness the substantial carbon sequestration and ecological rehabilitation potential of regenerative agriculture practices. The ongoing project aims to promote these practices among farms engaged in cultivating various crop combinations such as rice-wheat, maize-rice, rice, maize-wheat, cotton-wheat, cotton, sugarcane, millets and legumes. The project covers several states in India, including Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Assam, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu. The project interventions were implemented in the year 2020. Starting with 45 thousand hectares, the area will be stabilized at 16,58000 hectares in 2030 and maintained until 2040.

The “Santa Nicolasa North Patagonia Regenerative Grazing Project” aims to stop and reverse the historic soil degradation process of the region by implementing regenerative grazing technics by restoring the ecological condition of ~70.000 hectares of rangeland soils on Santa Nicolasa farm. Regenerative grazing activities can increase SOC concentrations, improve natural growing grasses, decrease bare soil, and improve water infiltration, among others. An average amount of 0,4% of Soil Organic Matter, is expected to increase, which results in a net GHG emissions reduction and removals of ~ 1,400,000 tCO2e in the SOC pool, with an annual average of 71,000 tCO2e in 20 years of the project. In general terms, the regenerative grazing activities restrict the cattle to relatively small paddocks to generate intensive grazing in short periods, followed by long grazing resting periods. As a result, a homogeneous disturbance on all the forage species is generated, avoiding the selectivity of the cattle for the most palatable plants. This technique requires the installation of new fencing and watering infrastructure and a significant adaptation of management practices. The project contributes to sustainable development by promoting an integrated management scheme with the ecosystem in privately owned land, avoiding carbon emissions and restoring native ecosystems from a degradation process together with the continuity of sustainable food production; promoting sustainable practices along the region, generating labor demand from the local population, and making improvements in infrastructure; generating knowledge on current SOC concentrations data and monitoring the effects of regenerative grazing management in the region; developing and improving a new mechanism to finance projects in the sustainable livestock production sector; the conservation of a unique ecosystem, that despite the severe degradation, still conserves the original land use and the natural ecosystem structure.

The Carbon Program by AGROROBÓTICA aims the recovery of degraded pasture and crops by adopting and maintaining several climate-smart agriculture practices and considering the specificity of each Brazilian biome: Amazon Forest, Cerrado, Caating, Atlantic Forest, Pampa, and Pantanal. In advance, it is expected to increase the sustainability of this sector and raising the life standards in rural areas. The reductions and removal of GHG emissions expected to be achieved would not have taken place without it. As this is a grouped project, as defined by the VCS standard, it includes multiple growers with multiple enrolled fields. The estimate is that the project could promote a GHG emission reduction and removal of up 2,624,400 tCO2eq promoted by more than 2,000,000 ha, in the next 20 years. The carbon credit payments will provide an additional source of income to help farmers to implement sustainable practices and improve the livelihoods of their communities. This project is an agricultural GHG emission reduction and removal project using the methodology “VM0042: Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management”, v. 2.0 and the AGLIBS ® Artificial Intelligence (AI) Platform, which is specifically addressed to fulfil the need for a high-integrity and cost-efficient monitoring system (MRV- measurable, reportable, and verifiable) through the emerging technology LIBS. The overall objective will be achieved by supporting farmers to adopt and maintain climate-smart agricultural practices through agronomic support and the monitoring of soil carbon stock change inside the farm boundary. The primary goal is to promote a range of regenerative agricultural land management practice improvements targeted to increase soil organic carbon (SOC) storage and reduce net emissions of CO2, CH4, and N2O from grower operations and degraded pasture area, increase farm resilience to extreme weather and climate change, and enhance yield, improve soil quality, and reduce GHG emissions.

THE PROJECT AIMS TO IMPLEMENT ALL FORMS OF IMPROVEMENT IN AGRICULTURE FROM THE CUTTING OF FERTILIZERS TO NO GRAZING AND TO USE AGRICULTURAL LANDS WHERE POSSIBLE AS EVERGREEN MEADOWS OR BETTER PERMANENT GRASSLANDS

Grow Indigo is implementing a project in Maharashtra and Gujarat to boost smallholder farmers' income through the adoption of regenerative agriculture, resulting in reduced greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and positive environmental and economic outcomes. The proposed project in Maharashtra and Gujarat addresses the GHG emissions caused by traditional agricultural practices in crops such as cotton, sugarcane, rice, wheat, maize, or soybean, without excluding other crops. Intensive agriculture practices in the project area have posed threats to land sustainability and contributed to increased GHG emissions. The project aims to promote regenerative agricultural practices, such as optimized fertilizer management, cover cropping, zero- or reduced-tillage, improved water management/ irrigation, crop rotation, and agroforestry, to restore soil health, enhance biodiversity, and improve productivity. The project takes an integrated and science-backed approach, including agricultural extension, outreach, agronomic support, digital data collection, and biogeochemical modeling. The project will initially target 40,000 hectares in the project area and cover diverse cropping systems with regenerative agricultural practices that are known to reduce GHG emissions (N2O, CO2e, and SOC) and thus generate carbon credits. The project also aims to link smallholder farmers to voluntary carbon markets, providing them with additional income opportunities and incentivizing the adoption of regenerative agriculture. With a cash incentive, smallholder farmers in the project boundary will adopt these practices more readily and contribute to sustainability and reduce GHG emissions. Through these efforts, the project seeks to contribute to sustainability, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and improve the overall livelihoods of smallholder farmers in the project area.

The project basically consists of the application of regenerative agriculture techniques and strategies on different farms in Spain, to promote a more sustainable agronomic management, and as a result increasing the amounts of atmospheric carbon fixed in the soil. Regenerative agriculture promotes practices such as the reduction or absence of tilling the soil, the presence of plant covers, the non-use of synthetic chemical products, organic fertilization, the optimization of water use, the improvement of by-products or waste management, and crop rotation, among others. The project is national scope and will be carried out on all those farms within the boundaries of the Spanish State that adopt the commitment to improve their agronomic management and that meet the established requirements. Regenerative agricultural management is focused on improving the soil’s properties and promoting conservation practices. The implementation of these measures will help to improve the health and fertility of agricultural soils which translates into an increase in the amount of organic matter (OM) in those soils. Carbon is one of the main components of OM, so increasing its percentage in soils is equivalent to increasing the amount of Soil Organic Carbon (SOC). Each of the regenerative strategies proposed in the project has a direct or indirect effect on the reduction of Green-house Gases (GHG), either by reducing emissions or by increasing its fixation in the soil. Although it is gaining ground in recent years, regenerative agriculture is not a common practice in the Spanish territory. Most farms are managed according to the principles of conventional agriculture, in which the soil is considered a mere support which generally has very little organic life and therefore, the amounts of OM and C are well below the levels that they could potentially contain. The Sustainable Farming Carbon Project in Spain will be developed as a grouped project.

According to information from the Ministry of the Environment of Japan, total GHG emissions from the agricultural sector in Japan in 2018 were about 32.3 million t-CO2eq. Of these, emissions from rice cultivation were the largest, at approximately 12 million t-CO2eq. , accounting for 38.2% of total emissions. The implementation of this project will reduce emissions by tCO2eq. per year and contribute to the reduction of GHG emissions from these agricultural activities. At this project, we use VM0042 to reduce CH4 by using no pesticides, no fertilizers, and by drying the soil in the middle of the year. As for environmental impact, the absence of chemical fertilizers reduces most of the nitrous oxide generated from the soil and the carbon dioxide produced during the production and transportation of fertilizers, and the absence of animal-based fertilizers eliminates concerns about methane emissions from the fertilizer production process.
