The Improved Grazing management in Mosaic Forest-Grasslands Landscapes in the centre-north of Argentina aims to remove greenhouse gases from the atmosphere by implementing regenerative grazing practices across different properties of the northern-central region of Argentina. The fundamental axis of this approach is the division of large pastures into smaller paddocks, implementing rotational grazing, which allows periods of rest and recovery for the land. The grouped project area covers 1,212,583 km2 in the north-center of Argentina. The region is dominated by grasslands with varying degrees of tree or shrub cover, ranging from savanna ecosystems characterized by sparse tree density to mosaic landscapes of grasslands and patches of native forests. These types of ecosystems, which integrate trees, forages, and livestock, can create significant synergies that improve soil health, while sequestering significant amounts of carbon from the atmosphere. Developing these regenerative grazing activities in areas with remnants of native trees or forests also plays and important role in the conservation of natural habitats. These productive systems mitigate climate change without the need for a change in land use, thereby safeguarding habitats that support a rich diversity of native flora and fauna. On this basis, the Project will in the future develop plans for biodiversity conservation and integration of the communities involved in each socio-ecosystem. In this way, conservation will be integrated into productive systems, encouraging landowners to change their paradigms about non-productive areas of ranches. The first Project Activity Instance is being carried out in the “La Alicia” property, located in the province of Santa Fe. The values obtained for this PAI determined that the project activities can result in a net GHG emissions reduction and removals of ~ 231,829 tCO2e in the SOC pool, with an annual average of 11,590 tCO2e in 20 years of the project.

The One Mara Carbon Project (OMCP) is an ecosystem-level conservation initiative that aims to protect ecological resources and provide economic and social co-benefits for communities by incentivizing conservancy formation and grassland restoration in the Maasai Mara landscape in Kenya. The goal of OMCP is to restore the degraded rangelands through improved grazing management and prevent further loss of grasslands by providing alternative livelihoods for communities, build resilient conservancies, ensure biodiversity conservation, and enhance tourism. This region is world-renown for the expansive rangelands where agropastoralists and wildlife co-exist. However, historical land sub-division into small, fenced land parcels and long term extensive grazing by livestock has led to land degradation, including the gradual loss in soil organic carbon (SOC). Communities living within the ecosystem depend on the condition of the grasslands to provide livelihoods that will meet their socio-economic needs. Implementing climate change mitigation measures and halting land degradation are vital to ensuring the longevity of this world-famous conservation area.

The project’s goal is to remove greenhouse gas (GHG) by implementing sustainable grazing management and controlled burning phases across the Limpopo - Lipadi (L-L) reserve. The baseline scenarios include loss of perennial grasses and destruction of indigenous trees and shrubs from wildlife grazing leading to erosion, soil carbon loss, water runoff and reduced wildlife carrying capacity. The project type that corresponds to the Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) is “Improved Grassland Management (IGM)” of the project category of “Agricultural Land Management (ALM)”. The project aims to increase soil organic carbon (SOC) through adjustment of burning and controlled grazing. The L-L wildlife conservation reserve covers an area of 20,712 hectares with all land units assembled from a contiguous group of traditional Botswana former cattle farms in the Tuli Block region. This area would establish phase 1 of a project that can incorporate further farms and common areas within the locale. A proposed phase 2 would see the project activities expanded to nearby cattle farms and game reserve areas, with the Limpopo-Lipadi team organizing the implementation of grassland management and/or controlled grazing techniques. Prior to the land becoming a wildlife conservation area, the farm was used for cattle ranching and limited cropping. There is overwhelming evidence of over grazing and the land when it was assembled in 2004 was severely degraded. This was compounded by drought and the conservation reserve had reached a tipping point in recent years, leading to further soil erosion and grassland degradation, to the detriment of the resident wildlife and ecosystem.

This project features implementation of rapid rotational grazing practices by dense aggregations of livestock to restore perennial grasses on degraded rangelands across 1.5 million hectares in southern Kenya. These new grazing practices are additional because they differ from the seasonal shifts in grazing activity from wet to dry season ranges and would not be possible without carbon revenues to support governance and monitoring of grazing activities. Rapid rotational grazing will enhance adaptation to climate change by improving soil water holding capacity, increasing surface water availability and providing grass banks as a hedge against drought. Habitat improvement from new grazing practices will restore wildlife corridors between iconic High Conservation Areas such as Serengeti, Kilimanjaro, Nairobi, and Tsavo National Parks and their associated ecosystems and enhance diversity of endemic taxa of plants, birds and insects. Finally, the project will provide direct benefits to 17 or more pastoralist communities in form of funds for bursaries to support women and the poorest community members as well as to construct water capture structures and infrastructure for delivering livestock to market. The project is expected to remove more than 63 million tons CO2e over the project lifetime of 40 years, or nearly 1.6 million tons CO2e a year on average.

The Livestock 2040/Uruguay project is driven and conceived by the consulting firm Profesionales SRL.It involves the participation of farmers in Uruguay who practice rotational grazing and have implemented good management practices on their property. Project is a grouped project.Rotational grazing is the primary activity of the project, which brings benefits to the ecosystem: it prevents and reduces soil erosion, improves the nutrient cycle, increases soil organic carbon (SOC) levels, and boosts pasture production. Participants also implement good practices in grass-fed livestock management with the goal of enhancing the ecosystem's well-being through the management of the plant-soil-animal relationship. Grazing management that enables higher quantity and quality of pasture to support high stocking rates while respecting animal welfare is a key component. Activities that increase biodiversity, such as the inclusion of native species and hunting prohibition, are considered relevant.Additionally, actions are proposed to reduce the use of external inputs, such as fertilizers or livestock feed, which contributes to decreasing greenhouse gas emissions. The result of these practices is an increase in organic matter in the soil, i.e., higher SOC content. Furthermore, the process of grassland degradation is reversed.The baseline consists of soils that were previously used for agriculture or extensive livestock farming. These soils have lost productive plant species, with areas of bare soil, compaction, low fertility, and a high risk of erosion.The project scenario consists of structured soils with a good amount of organic matter, high fertility levels, and enhanced plant growth. Compaction, erosion risk, and the amount of bare soil decrease.Estimations of emission reductions and absorption were made for the first project activity instant located in Sierra de las Animas, Maldonado, Uruguay. Greenhouse gas removals for this phase totaled 12,007 tCO2 over the 20 years.

The Enjipai Community Rangeland Carbon Project is a community run carbon project that incentivizes rangeland conservation and carbon storage through the adoption of improved rangeland management (IRM) in Arusha and Manyara regions of northern Tanzania. The Project builds upon prior work that has enabled local communities in the region to secure legal land tenure and develop sustainable livelihood opportunities. The Project is a grouped project that spans village lands that are the traditional home of pastoralist groups, primarily the Maasai, who have lived and kept livestock in the area for thousands of years. While historically nomadic, government policies enacted over the past 30 years have reduced pastoralists’ mobility by encouraging agriculture and settlement. This has resulted in increased grazing pressure on village rangelands and led to declines in rangeland health and soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks. Project partners began working with villages in the project area to establish land-use plans and secure legal protection of rangeland areas in 2015. Work then focused on the development of IRM plans that bunch and more livestock through a series of grazing blocks within village grazing areas to conserve forage and restore SOC stocks. IRM plans were first implemented in December 2021 for a cohort of villages, marking the carbon project start date. The project area at validation is expected to generate 18.6 million tCO2e of net removals on roughly 843,000 hectares over a 40-year crediting period. Removal rates are expected to be greater in the first 20 years and slow over time as SOC stocks saturate. The Project’s community benefits include strengthened land tenure and local governance, job creation, and increased forage productivity for community livestock. Biodiversity benefits are expected to include reduced rangeland conversion pressure, increased forage productivity for wildlife, and increased climate resilience through improved soil water holding capacity.

The Carbono Rural Paraguayan Chaco project aims to promote sustainable grazing practices in degraded pastures in Western Paraguay, targeting farmers practicing continuous or unsustainable grazing. The project aims to enhance grazing system productivity, soil carbon sequestration, and reduce GHG emissions. Paraguayan Chaco's primary economic activity is livestock farming, with farms ranging from 1,000 ha to 60,000 ha. Traditional management includes extensive pastures, resulting in degradation due to mismanagement, pests, weed proliferation, and overgrazing, mainly due to a lack of technical advice and high costs for sustainable practices. The project leverages carbon market incentives to promote sustainable farming. Current practices lead to severe pasture and soil degradation, reducing land productivity and carbon retention capacity. The project seeks to restore soil properties, prevent degradation, and increase livestock productivity through controlled grazing, pest and water management, and producer capacity building. Desde el Suelo, an agronomic extensionist team, will implement and monitor project activities. Increased grassland productivity is expected to sequester carbon, improve livestock production, and bring community and biodiversity benefits: i) enhance livestock production efficiency and stability, ii) improve soil quality, iii) raise livestock farming incomes, iv) enhance soil and grassland biodiversity, v) reduce pollution, vi) strengthen community resilience, vii) boost rural employment and skills in grazing management, viii) improve rural worker well-being, and ix) enhance animal welfare. The project aligns with UN Sustainable Development Goals: SDG Goal 2: Zero Hunger SDG Goal 8: Decent work and economic growth SDG Goal 13: Climate Action SDG Goal 15: Life on Land The project is a grouped initiative in Paraguayan Chaco, aiming to generate 445,697 tCO2e/year reductions and removals using Methodology VM0042 v2.0.

The “Bulgarian Sustainable Farming Carbon Project” aims to raise farmers' awareness on the benefits of regenerative agriculture and how changes in agricultural practices can help in climate change mitigation and adaptation. Regenerative agriculture land management practices refer to farming and grazing practices that aim to reverse climate change by rebuilding soil organic matter, sequestering carbon, improving degraded soil biodiversity, improving water cycle, and restoring soil fertility. Regenerative agriculture does not imply only one practice, instead, it is generally a combination of techniques. To achieve this objectives, different regenerative agricultural practices will be implemented. These will include, among others: - Promoting no tillage or minimal tillage: this practice aims to avoid soils tillage which is one of the main causes of soil losses/erosion. This practice helps not only to conserve the soil structure but also to improve it and improve the soil organic carbon levels. - Introducing cover crops: this practice aims to avoid having soils without vegetation cover by introducing alternative crops in-between the main productive ones. This promotes soils conservation by avoiding erosion. For this activity, Agrovar counts with a personalized information platform that processes the soils data which comes from laboratories and satellite information and as a result provides very specialized mixes of cover crops suggested for each land area according to every specific situation. - Information system for optimizing farming activities. The project is developed as a grouped project within the boundaries of Bulgaria. The project activity intends to add more instances over the upcoming years. The project implementation will result in an increase of carbon stocks and a reduction of GHG emissions.

Grow Indigo is implementing a regenerative agriculture-based carbon project in the extensive rice cultivation states of Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Odisha, and Telangana in India. The project area is characterized by traditional and intensive cultivation practices within diverse ecological systems, which emit significant amounts of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The southern region, encompassing Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Karnataka, excels in irrigated rice farming and cultivation in deltaic and non-deltaic regions. At the same time, Chhattisgarh and Odisha specialize in rainfed upland and lowland rice cultivation. Intensive agriculture practices in the project area have threatened food security and contributed to increased GHG emissions. The Grow Indigo project aims to incentivise farmers for adopting regenerative agriculture practices, thereby achieving the mitigation of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and fostering positive environmental and economic outcomes. Regenerative agriculture is a holistic farming system that focuses on improving soil health, biodiversity, and water quality. It can help to reduce GHG emissions by sequestering carbon in the soil. These practices include improved fertilizer management, cover cropping, crop rotation, reduced tillage, improved water management, crop residue management, agroforestry, etc. The project will also help to build the capacity of farmers to adopt regenerative agriculture practices through training and technical support. The project aims to scale up to 4 million hectares within the project area over a 5-year period. During the 20-year crediting period, it is estimated that there will be an average annual reduction and removal of 5,326,066 tCO2e. This innovative project has the potential to make a significant contribution to sustainable agriculture and climate change mitigation in India.

Grow Indigo is implementing a regenerative agriculture-based carbon project that spans across Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh. This project is taking a bold step towards environmental sustainability in the Ganga basin region of India. Common agricultural practice in these areas includes conventional methods such as heavy use of synthetic fertilizers, intensive tillage, crop residue burning, and excessive water consumption for irrigation. These practices have led to soil depletion and accelerated greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, threatening the ecosystem of the Ganga basin. The transition to regenerative agriculture is vital to counteract soil degradation, fertility loss, water pollution, and natural resource depletion. This shift is crucial to maintain the ecosystem services of the Ganga basin. The potential impact of the VCS carbon project is immense. It promises to significantly reduce GHG emissions, improve soil health, and enhance biodiversity. Beyond environmental benefits, the project aims to uplift the livelihoods of smallholder farmers and enhance the resilience of the Ganga basin ecosystem in the face of climate change. Over a five-year period, the project aims to scale up to cover 4 million hectares within the Ganga basin region of the project area. The 20-year crediting period is expected to yield an average annual emission reduction and removal of 5,048,425 tCO2e. Grow Indigo's efforts in this project exemplify a proactive and holistic approach to tackle environmental challenges, offering a ray of hope for the Ganga basin and its residents.

The project “Natural silvopastoral systems in the Colombian Orinoquia Region” is a grouped project comprising a set of activities to improve grassland management. The project primary objective is to achieve a reduction in overall emissions by focusing on carbon sequestration. This will be accomplished by enhancing livestock practices through the following project activities: - Implementation of adaptive multi-paddock grazing with improved deep-rooted grass cultivars, specifically Urochloa humidicola, - Human-assisted regeneration of arbustive chaparros (Curatella americana) on paddocks to harness the potential of existing natural processes of seed dispersal and resources to restore woody vegetation, - Cease grassland burns, and - Natural regeneration of tropical, highland savannah vegetation in buffer zones around riparian forests, and environmental. The project activities will take place in approximately 150,000 ha of Vichada and Meta, two of the four departments of the Orinoquia region in Colombia, referred to here as “Colombian Orinoquia”. The crediting period is 2020 to 2040 applying the VCS Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management VM0042 Version 2.0. An estimate of the annual average and total GHG emission reductions and removals are approximately 270,000 t CO2eq per year and 5,400,000 t CO2eq, respectively. With its implementation, project instances will see an increase in livestock production, alongside overall emissions reduction driven by soil carbon sequestration. Prior to the implementation of the project, livestock practices in the regions are characterized by annual burning of savannas and low-quality animal feed. It is also expected substantial contribution to the sustainable development goals (SDGs) 2 Zero hunger, 8 Decent work and economic growth, 9 Industry, innovation and infrastructure, 12 Responsible consumption and production, 13 Climate action, 15 Life on land, and 17 Partnerships for the goals.

C-Quest Capital’s Regenerative Agriculture and Forestry Technologies project aims to reverse the trends of soil and land degradation by promoting project activities that sequester carbon in agricultural soils and biomass; reduce dependency on nitrogen fertilizers; increase soil organic matter, moisture retention and health; reduce erosion; and diversify crop production and agricultural income streams. Specifically, this project will support conservation agriculture (CA), intercropping of leguminous shrubs, alley cropping, and farmer managed natural regeneration (FMNR) of trees on farmland across Malawi. CA includes adopting minimum or no-till practices, retaining crop residues, and rotating or intercropping multiple crops. Intercropping practices will focus mainly on Tephrosia vogelii, an indigenous fast growing, deep rooted leguminous shrub that can be used as green manure and produces abundant firewood. For alley cropping, multi-use trees or shrubs are planted in rows between crop strips to promote soil fertility and stability as well as diversify farm products. Lastly, FMNR practices vary widely according to the preferences of individual farmers but in general involve the selective protection of trees regenerating naturally from existing rootstock or stumps on croplands. Together, these practices transfer carbon from the atmosphere to above and belowground biomass through photosynthesis, a portion of which is further transferred to the SOC pool through biomass residues and root exudates. Reduced soil disturbance from no-till further protects SOC stocks, increased soil fertility reduces fertilizer use and its associated emissions, and crop residue retention avoids emissions from biomass burning.

BUFACAP is a national program that contributes to climate mitigation and adaptation efforts set out in the country’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) in the Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU) sector. It promotes sustainable agricultural land management on smallholder landholdings and is implemented across all administrative regions in the country, which fall within the Sudanian and Sudano-Sahelian Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZs). The main objectives are to sustainably increase smallholders’ agricultural productivity, food security, income, and welfare, build resilience /adaptation of the agrarian landscapes to climate change, reduce land degradation, and enhance tree/forest cover in line both the National Strategy for Soil Restoration, Conservation and Reclamation in Burkina Faso (SNRCRS) 2020-2024 and the National REDD+ agenda. The improved agricultural land management (IALM) practices promoted include compost/manure application, residue management (mulching), a menu of agroforestry, natural regeneration of trees, a menu of soil and water conservation practices, e.g., erosion control structures, a menu of integrated livestock management, e.g., forage crops, livestock housing, biogas digesters, etc., and a menu of agronomic practices, e.g., mixed cropping, intercropping, crop rotation, etc. The BUFACAP is a grouped project as defined in the VCS Standard version 4.5, i.e., “projects structured to allow the expansion of a project activity subsequent to project validation”. The project is using a partnership approach with the technical lead being the REDD+ Permanent Secretariat. The activities are expected to result in increased and sustainable agricultural production, tree/forest conservation and land restoration. GHG emission reductions will be generated through increased carbon storage in tree biomass and in soils within the agricultural landscapes. VM0042 will be used to account, monitor, and quantify the project’s GHG emission reductions.

The eAgronom Sustainable Farming in Central and Eastern Europe Project is an Agricultural Land Management (ALM) carbon offset project across Europe using the VM0042 methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management, version 2.0. The Project focuses on increasing the soil organic carbon in annual cropping systems. The Project seeks to drive the adoption of regenerative agricultural practices to promote carbon sequestration and reduce and remove GHG emissions.

The Carbon Smart Cropping and Pasture Systems USA II project is a grouped VCS AFOLU project open to perennial growers within the USA. The farms that will enroll in this project are growers of perennial crops that are mostly following traditional farming methods such as tilling, burning of crop residue and minimal cover crops and organic amendments. Crops may include but are not limited to fruit trees and nut trees. For this grouped project, greenhouse gas (GHG) reductions and removals will be achieved by the implementation of a combination of practice changes, including application of organic materials and mulch to reduce the reliance on synthetic fertilizers and to improve soil health; cover cropping and inter-row biomass generation; establishment of permanent tree crops; improved water management; and others. The undertaking of this project will support a number of United Nations Sustainable Development Goals in the project area, local communities, surrounding environments, and in the supply chain. The project will contribute towards SDG 2: Zero Hunger, SDG 12: Responsible Consumption and Production, and SDG 13: Climate Action.

Renove ALM Brazil project is committed to incorporating the Climate-smart Livestock Production (CSLP) approach into cattle ranches of the Minerva Foods supply chain to enhance their resilience and contribution to mitigating climate change. Through stakeholder involvement and collaborative actions, the project offers technical support for adopting sustainable livestock management practices and access to the voluntary carbon market. Based on the CSLP approach, the Renove ALM Brazil Project is structured in four main initiatives: i) sustainable pasture management, ii) improved herd management, iii) improved ranch management, and iv) project policies against native ecosystem degradation. As a result, the project expects to enhance the productivity and profitability of livestock production, improve the resilience and financial health of ranches, increase food security, and recognize ranchers that align livestock production with native ecosystems conservation. In addition, the project intends the removal of 3,565,727.00 tCO2eq through increased stocks of Soil Organic Carbon and the reduction of 60,391.00 tCO2eq of methane from enteric fermentation.

The Improved Agriculture Land Management Project in Argentina aims to support sustainable agricultural practices in the Central and Northern Region of Argentina. The Project will seek to implement practices that are currently not or only partially implemented in the country with low rates. Agricultural activities play a central role in the grouped project area. The current agricultural system is based on simplified farming practices. These include low crop rotation, monocultures and a high dependence on chemical inputs, which has led to soil degradation and nutrient depletion. The project will implement or intensify some of the following practices: (1) crop rotation, (2) rotations between agricultural and livestock practices, (3) cover crops, (4) implementation of regenerative livestock practices, (5) improvement of pasture management, (6) application of organic amendments, (7) improvement of water management or irrigation, and/ or (8) forest strips plantation. In addition, these activities will contribute to (1) minimize tillage and (2) minimize the introduction of crops that require soil disturbance in the harvesting process. These practices aim to increase soil organic matter, reduce soil erosion, promote the fixation and recycling of nutrients, prevent the spread of soil diseases, and maintain soil fertility in the long term, among other positive environmental effects. The first Project Activity Instance is being carried out in the province of Buenos Aires, comprising a total of 2,691 hectares. A very conservative estimate was made based on the projection of increasing the soil organic matter by 0.55% in 20 years. This is equivalent to an increase of 2.07 TCO2eq/ha-1year-1. Thus, the project activities can result in a net GHG emissions reduction and removals of ~ 108,608 tCO2e, with an annual average of 5,430 tCO2e in 20 years of the project.

The Rivulis Climate Row Crops in Europe (RCRC) grouped project aims to create a new sustainable farming approach for seasonal crops in Southern Europe. The first instances of the project are located in Northern Italy and focus on crops such as tomatoes, corn and more. The project is led by Rivulis Climate, as part of a global initiative developed by Rivulis, a leader in climate and irrigation solutions, to support the agriculture transition to more sustainable farming practices. The goals of this new initiative are as follows: a) Reduce greenhouse gases emissions by adopting more efficient irrigation methods such as drip-irrigation and decreasing usage of synthetic fertilizers through the use of fertigation solutions and organic fertilizers, b) Increase carbon storage in soils through the implementation of soil conservation practices such as cover crops, minimal tillage and better residue management, c) reduce water usage and d) improve long-term crop yields and soil health. The project is developed according to VCS methodology - VM0042 Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management - and falls under VCS Sectoral Scope 14, AFOLU.

The Carbon Smart Cropping and Pasture Systems USA project is a grouped VCS AFOLU project open to regenerative row crop farmers and graziers within the USA. The farms that will enrol in this project are growers and graziers that have mostly been following traditional farming methods such as tilling, removal of crop residue, no or minimal cover crops and with a strong reliance on chemical inputs, but who are now motivated to reduce their impact on the environment. For this grouped project, greenhouse gas (GHG) reductions and removals will be achieved by the implementation of a combination of practice changes, including the application of organic amendments and supplements, such as mulch and compost to reduce the reliance on synthetic fertilisers and to improve soil health, cover cropping, pasture improvement, improvement of herd management and grazing practices, improved water use efficiency and others. The undertaking of this project will support a number of United Nations Sustainable Development Goals in the project area, local communities, surrounding environments, and in the supply chain. The project will contribute towards SDG 2: Zero Hunger, SDG 12: Responsible Consumption and Production, and SDG 13: Climate Action.

Groundwork BioAg Rootella Carbon Agricultural Program (the ‘Project’) enables the adoption of improved agricultural land management (IALM) practices on continental United States and Canada, where the project instances and baseline scenarios of similar nature. The project developer (Groundwork BioAg) will facilitate this adoption through financial incentives and technical support. Landowners and tenant farmers (‘farmers’) will improve soil carbon sequestration rates by applying one or more of the following practices to increase soil carbon sequestration rates and/or reduce on-farm greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions: • Soil Amendments or seed treatments • Reduced Tillage and Stubble Management: • Cover Crops • Fertilizer Nitrogen Reductions • Energy Consumption Reductions through Practice Changes • Improved Crop Rotation • Methane Emission Reductions The focus of the Project is farmers who grow crops such as, but not limited to, corn, soy or wheat using conventional farming practices. These practices vary from farm to farm but may include one or more tillage passes per year, fields are generally left bare over winter, and excessive fertilizer application.

The Brazil Precision Agriculture Carbon Program (BPACP) incentivizes the large-scale adoption of big data-driven precision agriculture in Brazil. It is a grouped VCS project implemented by a national carbon credit cooperative society (“Carbon Coop”). The project has partnered with multiple stakeholders on a national scale, including soil laboratories, a big data analytics platform, agro-inputs and machinery dealers, local agricultural consultants and soil sampling experts, to connect with farmers and leverage the adoption of precision agriculture. The carbon project intends to harness data analytics, remote sensing, climate and crop modelling, artificial intelligence, and in-field sensors, to help farmers make data-informed decisions that sustainably increase productivity and crop resilience (adaptation), reduce and remove greenhouse gas emissions (mitigation), and enhance achievement of global food security and national development goals.

The Fortaleza Ituxi III ALM project is located in one of the regions with the highest deforestation rate in the Amazon Biome: the municipality of Lábrea. For the last 10 years, it has been one of the most deforested municipalities in the Amazon Biome and the south of Lábrea has already been reached by the “Arc of Deforestation”. Beside the damage caused to natural ecosystems, the land-use changes have provoked severe social conflicts through processes of land-grabbing and installation of agriculture and cattle ranching activities (often irregular or even illegal), contributing to the expulsion of family-scale forest extractives from that region. The main activity of the Fortaleza Ituxi III ALM project consists of growing Açaí (Euterpe oleracea) in an integrated production system intercropped with pasture for a low carbon cattle grazing. The project area is located in the municipality of Lábrea, in the state of Amazonas, in northern Brazil. The project area covers an extension of 371.52 ha, referring to the lease of the first instance and lies to the north of the Ituxi River, situated on the Nossa Senhora das Cachoeiras do Ituxi farm. The Fortaleza Ituxi III ALM is an Agriculture Land Management (ALM) project based on Improved Grassland Management (IGM) and it aims to include practices that demonstrably reduce net GHG emissions of grassland ecosystems by increasing soil carbon stocks, improving aboveground biomass and reducing N2O emissions and/or reducing CH4 emissions. The estimated GHG emission reduction is 58,099.93 tCO2e over the 20-year project lifetime (01-July-2023 to 30-June-2043), with an annual average of 2,905.00 tCO2e.

The Mafisa Livestock Grazing Carbon Project (MLGCP) is proposed by ZayoHub, a Zambian non-profit. The project aims to generate carbon credits through enhanced grazing and fire management, utilizing VM0032 methodology, (Adoption of Sustainable Grasslands through Adjustment of Fire & Grazing). It will monitor activities and impacts through on-the-ground livestock tracking by grazing coordinators and via remote impact assessment via satellite imagery. The initiative focuses on empowering impoverished local communities residing in mopane and miombo woodlands in southwestern Zambia. In this region, soils are poor; farming is largely subsistence-based and highly marginal, and cattle rearing is the dominant historical land use. Key aspects of long-standing traditional farming practices reflect the principles of rotational grazing and good fire management, but their use has lapsed in recent decades. Improving animal husbandry on sustainably managed rangelands is a significant opportunity for sustainable livelihoods in the project area. However, at present animals are usually not herded, contributing to degradation of grassland degradation. High tick-borne disease prevalence and other parasites greatly impede productivity. MLGCP promotes cattle grazing rotations to restore traditional grazing practices, simulate wild herbivores' migratory patterns, and foster grassland regeneration. Additionally, it targets the reduction of burning frequency, enhancing carbon storage. MLGCP will provide animal health services for farmers participating in collective planned grazing. Anticipating annual net removals of 1 ton of CO2e/ha, the project plans to expand from 220,000 ha initially to 1.26 million ha by 2030. Projected annual carbon credit yields are set to rise from 220,000 tons CO2e in 2024 to around 1.26 million tons CO2e by 2029, sustaining until 2063. Overall, MLGCP aims to remove over 47 million tons CO2e, contributing to long-term atmospheric carbon reduction.

This project features implementation of rapid rotational grazing practices by dense aggregations of livestock to restore perennial grasses on degraded rangelands across 970,685 hectares in northern Tanzania. These new grazing practices are additional because they differ from the currently practiced seasonal shifts in grazing activity from wet to dry season ranges, and the new practices would not be possible without carbon revenues to support governance and monitoring of grazing activities. Rapid rotational grazing will enhance adaptation to climate change by improving soil water holding capacity, increasing surface water availability and providing grass banks as a hedge against drought. Habitat improvement from new grazing practices will result in biodiversity benefits in the form of improved habitat inside wildlife corridors between iconic High Conservation Areas such as Serengeti, Kilimanjaro, Nairobi, and Tsavo National Parks and their associated ecosystems and enhance diversity of endemic taxa of plants, birds and insects. Finally, the project will provide direct benefits to dozens of pastoralist communities in form of funds for bursaries to support women and the poorest community members as well as to construct water capture structures and infrastructure for delivering livestock to market. The project is expected to remove more than 62 million tons CO2e over the project lifetime of 40 years, or more than 1.5 million tons CO2e a year on average.

The Regenerative Agriculture Project for Eastern European Soils, referred to here as the Project, is an Agricultural Land Management (ALM) carbon project developed and owned by eAgronom, implementing project activities in Ukraine and Moldova. It follows Verra’s VM0042 methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management, version 2.0, hereafter called VM0042. The Project is dedicated to enhancing soil organic carbon levels in arable lands (which include annual croplands, temporary grasslands - i.e. grass species within a crop rotation - and fallows), perennial croplands, and permanent grasslands. Its primary goal is to encourage the adoption of regenerative agricultural practices that foster carbon sequestration while minimising and eliminating greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Some files are uploaded by the Project Proponent for the purpose of project listing and may not have been reviewed, validated, or verified by either a VVB or Verra. Please refer to the Registration and Issuance Process v5.0 for project listing rules and requirements.

Brazilian ALM Carbon Program in different crop use and pasture integrated system aims the agricultural GHG emission reduction and removal by adopting improved ALM practices and considering the specificity of each Brazilian biome, following the “VM0042: Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management”, v. 2.0 and the AGLIBS ® Artificial Intelligence (AI) Platform, which is specifically addressed to fulfil the need for a high-integrity and cost-efficient monitoring system (MRV- measurable, reportable, and verifiable) through the emerging technology LIBS. The overall objective will be achieved by supporting farmers to adopt and maintain climate-smart agricultural practices through agronomic support and the monitoring of soil carbon stock change inside the farm boundary. The primary goal is to promote a range of regenerative agricultural land management practice improvements targeted to increase soil organic carbon (SOC) storage and reduce net emissions of CO2, CH4, and N2O from grower operations and degraded pasture area, increase farm resilience to extreme weather and climate change, and enhance yield, improve soil quality, and reduce GHG emissions. The reductions and removal of GHG emissions expected to be achieved would not have taken place without it. As this is a grouped project, as defined by the VCS standard, it includes multiple growers with multiple enrolled fields. The estimate is that the project could promote a GHG emission reduction and removal of up 1,816,666 tCO2eq promoted by more than 2,000,000 ha, in the next 20 years. In advance, it is expected to increase the sustainability of this sector and raising the life standards in rural areas.

Climate Investment Partners LLC, in partnership with Entooma Sidai Limited, aims to restore over 650,000 hectares of degraded grasslands in Narok County, Kenya via the Entooma Sidai: A Maasai Mara Rangeland Restoration and Conservation Project. The Project is estimated to generate approximately 689,731 net Verified Carbon Units (VCUs) annually over a 40-year project period for a total of over 27 million VCUs. The Project is being developed using the Verified Carbon Standard’s (VCS) VM0032 Methodology for the Adoption of Sustainable Grasslands through Adjustment of Fire and Grazing, v1.0. Continued overgrazing in the project area has degraded grasslands and rangelands, reduced grass biodiversity, inhibited grassland regeneration, reduced grass seed banks, increased the spread of invasive species, and decreased the availability of viable forage for both livestock and wildlife. The promotion of planned rotational grazing of livestock will restore degraded grasslands and increase grassland carbon stocks by allowing grasses and plants to recover and regenerate between grazes, which in turn will aid with increasing soil carbon through increasing plant productivity and limiting soil organic matter losses. Overall, the expected impacts of widespread implementation of sustainable grazing management practices are: climate change mitigation, adaptation and increased resiliency; reduced soil erosion and run-off; reduced loss of livestock; improved water infiltration and soil health; increased household income and food security; and the expansion of wildlife habitats and increased biodiversity.

East Africa Soil and Biodiversity improvement project in Eastern Africa is a voluntary carbon project that implements Agricultural Land Management (ALM) practices developed and owned by eAgronom. This initiative is currently underway in Rwanda, Kenya, and Tanzania, with the potential for further expansion into neighbouring countries. It follows Verra's VM0042 methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management, version 2.0, referred to as VM0042, the project is dedicated to enhancing soil organic carbon levels within annual cropping systems. The project aims to spread adoption of regenerative agricultural practices, ultimately leading to increased carbon sequestration. By doing so, it seeks to improve soil health and deliver significant benefits to farmers. Simultaneously, the project is driven to sequester greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The Regenerative Agriculture Project in Eastern Africa focuses on elevating soil health, benefiting farmers, and mitigating greenhouse gas emissions and build agricultural resilience. By initiating positive changes in East Africa and contemplating expansion, the project holds the potential to become a catalyst for transformative practices in the broader region.

In the context of carbon removal, the BRA-3C Project seeks to implement sustainable soil management practices, highlighting crop rotation to guarantee the diversification of commercial crop, cover cropping to maximize land use through the sowing of two crops in a single season, and the maintenance of plant residues and living plants in the soil, promoting carbon retention, and strengthening soil fertility. Regarding emissions, the project promotes the spread of biologicals as soil conditioners, which include fungal and microbial inoculants. Their use is expected to contribute to soil health improvement, besides establishing control over the nitrogen application's timing and dosage. The BRA-3C Project aims to increase soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks and adopt input management mechanisms to reduce emissions from agricultural activities in the Cerrado biome. The project aims to implement sustainable intensification practices for agricultural land use, to increase land and food productivity, while also expanding the conservation of natural resources. In total, the BRA-3C Project is estimated to produce 10,361,853.33 tCO2e, with an annual average of approximately 259,046.33 tCO2e/year. The grouped project location includes the geographical extension of the Cerrado Biome within the geographic boundaries of Brazil.

Tiryaki Agro is a global agro commodity company with 25 production sites across 11 countries. Tiryaki Agro is leading agricultural supply chain company in the region by sourcing from more than 35 countries. Tiryaki Agro' is planning to implement and widen the regenerative and organic carbon practices in the agricultural areas under control. Proposed project will be implemented in Alparslan Farm located in Muş Province of Turkiye, which occupies around 6,000 ha land. Tiryaki grows wheat, sunflower, sugarbeet and other agricultural in this land. Tiryaki and GTE are collaborating to calculate and certify the emission reduction from those activities and replicate this practices in new agricultural areas via funding expected from carbon revenues.

The project Farm Resilience and Regeneration in France and Belgium aims to transform agriculture by empowering and supporting farmers to transition to regenerative practices. It offers robust instruments to enable corporations to contribute to nature regeneration, with a focus on carbon sequestration, biodiversity, and water resources. Spanning arable farming, livestock, mixed crop-livestock systems, and vineyards across mainland France and Belgium, the initiative focuses on creating resilient farms through ecosystem and soil revival. Utilizing the VM0042 methodology for Improved Agriculture and Land Management (ALM) and Quantification Approach 1: Measure and Model, the project targets 3,100 farms over the 20-year crediting period, transforming 460,000 hectares. It conservatively anticipates average annual carbon removals of 428,000 tCO2e, totaling 8,600,000 tCO2e over the crediting period. With tailored agronomic and financial support, rigorous monitoring, and a results and measure-based model, the project targets net carbon removals for VCUs while contributing to multiple UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), including improved access to knowledge for small-scale farmers (SDG 2), enhanced gender inclusion (SDG 5), increased water-use efficiency (SDG 6), improved resource efficiency (SDG 8), reduced chemical releases (SDG 12), climate change mitigation (SDG 13), land restoration (SDG 15), and fostering partnerships between industry and farmers (SDG 17). By investing in this project, you are contributing to the future of agriculture, benefiting both farmers and ecosystems, and making your business regenerative.

The proposed project ‘MZURI methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management’ aims to reduce and sequester GHG emissions by implementing more sustainable agricultural practices on fields in northern Poland. The planned schedule of activities fits within Verra’s VM0042 standard, which comprises a range of regenerative agricultural land management practice changes targeted at reducing net emissions of CO2, CH4, and N2O by grower operations and increasing soil organic carbon (SOC) storage. This is being achieved in this project by supporting farmers to implement climate-smart agricultural land management practices through the use of innovative land machines and integrated improved agricultural practices, supported by digital data collection tools and modelling. These practices include reductions in fertilizer use, strip tillage, adapted crop rotations, and cover cropping. Overall, these practice changes seem well appropriate to reduce emissions from agricultural production, to increase farm resilience to extreme weather events and the effects of climate change, and to promote increased soil (micro-) biological diversity. Expected co-benefits of the project (other than carbon reduction and sequestration) are expressed along the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Considering the context and location of the project, its scope of activities will contribute to the achievement of: • SDG 2 (Zero Hunger), • SDG 3 (Good Health and Wellbeing), • SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), • SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure), • SDG 13 (Climate Action), • SDG 15 (Life on Land). The project’s scope of activities significantly lowers the GHG emissions of agricultural activities vs. baseline scenario, and enhances or restores the carbon storage capacity of the area, thereby sequestering CO2 from the atmosphere. The project meets the criteria for climate additionality as well as community and biodiversity additionality, and shows a regulatory surplus.

This grouped project in the Kunene Highlands Elephant Landscape in Namibia aims to work in partnership with 12 Community Conservancies to expand regeneration and conservation efforts, promoting sustainable land management practices and livelihoods. The landscape, representing almost 1 million hectares, is an area of considerable ecological importance, providing biodiversity connectivity between adjacent national parks. It also holds a significant elephant population, and overlaps with ranges of at least 3 species listed as critically endangered, 10 listed as endangered, 12 listed as vulnerable, and 10 listed as near threatened by the IUCN, including large megafauna and birds that are at high risk of habitat loss, poaching and climate change threats. Through regenerative rangeland management, the project will support grassland restoration, carbon sequestration, soil moisture retention and climate resilience.

This grouped project implements sustainable grazing practices on ranching lands in the state of Montana, USA. The rangeland landscape includes grasslands, steppe, prairies and forests. Wildlife characteristic of the area includes grizzly bears, pronghorn antelope, bison, white-tailed deer, elk and bighorn sheep. The land management practice changes will restore grasslands, increase vegetation cover, foster native plant diversity, sequester carbon, improve water infiltration, and reduce runoff. These impacts will increase the climate resilience of the ranches and support rancher livelihoods.

This project takes place in the state of Coahuila, Mexico, with the goal of restoring lands which have been extensively degraded by overgrazing. These lands are being overrun by invasive species such as desert shrubs, cacti, annual grasses and forbs. The project implements sustainable grazing practices aimed at restoring grasslands, increasing vegetation cover, sequestering carbon, improving water infiltration, and reducing runoff. These impacts will increase the climate resilience of the ranches and support rancher livelihoods. These are biodiversity-rich areas, featuring black bears, bobcats, coyotes, cougars, and golden eagles, among other species.

Bundelkhand, straddling between Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh in India, faces severe challenges such as drought, land degradation, water scarcity, erratic rainfall, soil erosion, and unsustainable practices, making it one of the most formidable regions in the country. The project area comprises a total of 8 districts; Chhatarpur, Hamirpur and Niwari districts in Madhya Pradesh and Chitrakoot, Jhansi, Lalitpur, Mahoba, and Tikamgarh in the state of Uttar Pradesh. The challenges in these districts and the Bundelkhand region are compounded by water stress, primarily caused by insufficient and erratic rainfall, high runoff rates, and poor soil water retention capacity, leading to declining soil fertility and productivity. To tackle these challenges, the project proponent is dedicated to promoting enhanced Agriculture Land Management (ALM) and improved agroforestry practices. These practices encompass a range of interventions, including improved fertilizer management, cover cropping, crop rotation, enhanced water management, effective crop residue management, and incorporation of agroforestry plantations, among others.

The proposed VCS IALM (Improved Agricultural Land Management) project activity aims at developing a carbon sequestration project in the context of Organic farming adoption and certification by Qmark Foundation for Sustainable Livelihood Development (herein referred as Qmark Foundation) and it is also eliminating the dependency on chemical fertilizers and pesticides by replacing those with environment-friendly organic-based soil amendments. The Qmark Foundation is promoting the adoption and organic certification of Organic farming practices on approximately 1,00,000 ha in first project instance in Uttar Pradesh and other states in India. Further future instances will be added.

The BASF Brazilian Carbon Farming project is a program developed by BASF Agricultural Solutions as part of the Global Climate Smart Farming Initiative, which promotes the implementation of sustainable agricultural practices across a broad network of farms. The main outcomes of this project include increasing the adoption of sustainable agricultural practices that reduce and/or remove GHG emissions in Brazil, while maintaining or increasing crop yield. The increased adoption of regenerative agricultural practices will contribute to a more sustainable and resilient agricultural system. This grouped project uses version 2.0 of the VM0042 Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management as the main guidance document and adheres to the corrections and clarifications of VM0042, V2.0.

Traditional rice farming practices involve the continuous flooding of fields through the crop’s growing period. But when rice paddies are flooded, the soil environment favors methanogenesis. By changing the water management of rice paddies from continuously flooded to intermittently flooded, there is reduced anaerobic decomposition of organic matter in the soil, leading to a decrease in methane emissions. This technique is called 'alternate wetting and drying' (AWD); it is a periodic drying and re-flooding irrigation scheduling approach in which the fields are allowed to dry for a few days before re-irrigation. This method reduces greenhouse gas emissions and irrigation water demand, without reducing crop yields. The Upper Pampanga River Climate-Smart Rice Project is an initiative to transform conventionally flooded irrigated rice production to AWD to achieve emissions reductions, as well as community and biodiversity benefits. The Project will be implemented in Central Luzon in the Upper Pampanga River Integrated Irrigation Systems (UPRIIS) service area of the National Irrigation Administration (NIA), located approximately 150 km north of Manila, and spanning approximately 143,500 hectares over the provinces of Nueva Ecija, Tarlac, Pampanga, and Bulacan. The Project is expected to result in 1,952,264 tons of GHG emissions reductions (CO2-equivalent) over the initial 7-year crediting period. Specific project interventions include: 1. Training farmers on implementation of AWD which delivers appropriate knowledge in field preparation, irrigation, drainage, and use of fertilizer. 2. Provision of incentives to farmers for participating in the AWD program through a benefit-sharing agreement. 3. GHG monitoring, and monitoring for community and biodiversity benefits. 4. Capacity-building with local stakeholders including the National Irrigation Administration (NIA), UPRIIS staff, Local Government staff, and local Irrigators Associations (IAs).

The project activity aims to reduce reliance on chemical fertilizers by substituting them with organic soil amendments. Through practices such as mulching, compost integration, and vermicompost manure, the project seeks to enhance soil carbon sequestration and nutrient levels. This Sustainable Agricultural Land Management (SALM) initiative anticipates reducing greenhouse gas emissions by minimizing nitrous oxide release from synthetic chemical fertilizers by replacing them with environmentally friendly organic fertilizers. The project aims to improve soil organic carbon levels and minimize methane emissions by managing post-harvest crop residue. The project supports smallholder farmers in transitioning to organic farming methods, improving their resilience to climate change while enhancing agricultural productivity.

The Gut&Bösel – Living Soils Initiative is an innovative venture aimed at transforming conventional agricultural practices into sustainable and resilient farming ecosystems in Germany. Gut&Bösel is an agricultural operation dedicated to addressing global challenges such as climate change, biodiversity loss, and food security. Through a comprehensive suite of sustainable farming practices—including reduced-till farming, year-round soil cover, diverse crop rotations, on-farm compost production, intercropping, holistic grazing, and agroforestry — the project aims to enhance soil fertility, boost biodiversity, and regenerate entire ecosystems. The Project targets the shortcomings of traditional agriculture in Germany, where extensive monoculture farming dominates the landscape. The heavy reliance on synthetic fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides, have led to significant soil degradation, biodiversity loss, and increased erosion. These methods prioritize short-term yields at the expense of long-term soil health, making farms increasingly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change and threatening their economic viability. Through its implementation, the project aims to achieve significant greenhouse gas emission (GHG) reductions and carbon dioxide removals. These methods reduce soil disturbance, increase soil organic matter, and capture carbon through enhanced biomass growth. Over its lifetime, the project is expected to generate approximately 9,192,300 tCO2e in GHG reductions, equivalent to an annual average of 230,000 tCO2e. The Gut&Bösel – Living Soils Initiative sets a new benchmark for sustainable agriculture in Germany, demonstrating the potential for a healthy, self-sustaining agroecosystem that balances soil health, nutrient cycles, and biodiversity with productivity. This model serves as a crucial example of climate change mitigation and adaptation solutions, offering insights that are vital for farmers across Germany and Europe in the coming decades.

The agricultural land management (ALM) projects aim to mitigate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions (CO2, CH4 and N2O) by avoiding the burning of residue and also offset the CO2 emissions by adopting improved ALM practices like residue incorporation & retention. Offsetting emissions from the dominant rice-wheat cropping system through residue management would strengthen the role of agriculture in VCM to reduce the country’s net emissions by 2030. This will also improve air quality by decreasing seasonal emissions of black carbon and respirable particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), mitigating severe short-term and irreversible long-term threats to health and the environment in the Indo-Gangetic plains. In addition, the adoption of residue management practices will provide direct monetary benefits to the farmer with co-benefits of improved soil health and crop productivity.

Paddy fields are the most dominant anthropogenic sources of methane in the atmosphere (5-20% of the total emission from all anthropogenic sources). Anaerobic decomposition of organic material in flooded rice fields produces methane, which escapes the atmosphere primarily by transport through the rice plants. The annual CH4 emitted from a given rice area is a function of the number and duration of crops grown, water regimes before and during the cultivation period, and organic and inorganic soil amendments. Soil type, temperature, and rice cultivar also affect CH4 emissions. This CH4 emission-intensive cultivation method will be targeted by the proposed programme, which will involve implementing the technology/measures that result in reduced anaerobic decomposition of organic matter in rice cropping soils and, thus, reduced methane generation. The project activity comprises of grouped projects of rice fields implementing the following methods: a) Drum Seeded Rice (DSR) with minimal tillage against transplanted rice cultivation b) Alternate wetting and Drying Irrigation (AWDI) against conventional flood irrigation in rice

This complex nexus necessitates the estimation of carbon emissions from groundwater irrigation. Rajan et al. (2020) showed that groundwater irrigation emits 45.3–62.3 MMT of carbon annually (the data seems doubtful; we need to check), contributing 8–11% of India's total carbon emission. This analysis showed that deep tube wells have a huge carbon footprint, and their growing number is a serious environmental concern. Currently, our country accounts for one-fourth of the global groundwater extraction (i.e. 251 km3/year) and uses 90% of the abstracted groundwater for irrigation. Groundwater provides irrigation to around 40–45 million hectares of cultivated land, which is about 60% of the total irrigated area in the Country. Besides stressing the groundwater reserves, intensive groundwater pumping has resulted in higher energy consumption sourced from electricity or fossil fuels, resulting in higher carbon emissions. Judicious and efficient use of water through micro-irrigation can solve the twin problem of accelerated loss of groundwater and reduction of CO2 emissions. Therefore, there is a need to identify practices for efficient water management strategies for different crops and cropping systems and associated GHG emissions. With this background, a project is being proposed with the following specific objectives: i. To evaluate water and fertilizer savings under micro-irrigation in different agroecological regions of India. ii. To estimate GHG reduction associated with fertilizer and water saving through micro-irrigation.

This agricultural land management (ALM) projects aims to reduce the greenhouse gas (GHG) emission and removals CO2 resulting from the adoption of improved ALM practices. The project involves adoption of natural farming that is compatible with regenerative agriculture and has a particular focus on increasing soil organic carbon (SOC) storage. This will involve management practices that maintain or enhance SOC affect soil quality and may favour the capacity of soils to sequester further organic carbon. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of these measures depends upon both the soil characteristics and the current SOC content. The Projects introduce or implement one or more new changes to pre-existing ALM practices which: a) Improve organic fertilizer management; b) Improve water/irrigation management; c) Reduce tillage/improve residue management; d) Improve crop planting and harvesting (e.g., improved agroforestry, mix cropping, crop rotations, cover crops); and/or The project is initiated in Gujarat and it is today defined as having seven universal principles that can work in different contexts: • Soil to be covered with crops for all 365 days in a year • Minimal disturbance of soil (zero or minimum tillage) • Use of indigenous seed • Diverse crops and trees • Integrate animals into farming • Increase organic residues on the soil (Mulching) • Pest and disease management through botanical extracts

Technologies to be Implemented by the project 1. High-Density Planting System in cotton to capture more CO2 from the atmosphere: This is an innovative planting system standardised by ICAR-CICR, Nagpur, wherein on light soils, plant density will be optimised up to 75000/ha, thereby increasing cotton productivity and cotton biomass as a whole. Moreover, in High-Density Planting System (HDPS) cotton, more emphasis will be given to the reduction in GHG emissions through the introduction of environmentally friendly cotton cultivation practices. 2. Canopy management in cotton: With the help of mepiquat chloride, canopy management will be done, which in turn enhances radiation use efficiency and better portioning of photosynthate and finally improves the harvest index and seed cotton yield. 3. Shredding, incorporation of cotton stalk to store organic carbon in the soil: Avoidance of burning of cotton stalk wherever it is a common practice after cotton picking. After the harvest of cotton, the cotton stalk will be shredded into small pieces and incorporated into the soil. For the rapid decomposition of the cotton stalk addition of microbial consortia will be done. This could facilitate the enhancement of soil organic carbon by crop residue recycling.

This Agricultural Land Management (ALM) project aims to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions (CO2, CH4, and N2O) resulting from conventional/pre-existing agricultural land management practices. The project involves the adoption of improved agricultural practices that are compatible with regenerative agriculture and has a particular focus on increasing soil organic carbon (SOC) storage and GHG emission reduction. This will involve management practices that maintain or enhance SOC, affect soil quality, and may favour the capacity of soils to sequester further organic carbon. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of these measures depends upon both the soil characteristics and the current SOC content. The Projects introduce or implement one or more new changes to pre-existing ALM practices, which: a) Improved fertilizer (organic or inorganic) management; b) Reduce tillage/improve residue management; d) Improve crop planting and harvesting (e.g., improved crop rotations, cover crops) The project was initiated in Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh) and Ranjnandgaon (Chhattisgarh). It is today defined as having seven principles that can work in different contexts: • Reduced tillage • Avoidance of crop residue burning • Recycling crop residue through composting (vermicompost/windrow composting) • Improved/diversified crop rotation • Increase organic input in the soil • Reduce synthetic fertilizer input • Soil to be covered with cover crops throughout the year The project activity is implemented in about 60 hectares in the first phase in Bhopal District of Madhya Pradesh and Rajnadgaon district of Chhattisgarh.

The project aims to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and remove (CH4 and N2O) resulting from the adoption of improved Agricultural Land Management (ALM) practices. The project involves the adoption of Direct Seeded Rice (DSR), Precision N management (Real-time application of N fertilisers using Customised Leaf Color Chart (CLCC) and Rice Crop Manager (RCM) software, Green manure (Dhaincha) incorporation and application of Liquid formulation of endophytic and rhizospheric nitrogen-fixing bioinoculants) and Water Management (Pani Pipe/Sensor based AWD) that is compatible with regenerative agriculture and has a particular focus on minimising GHG emissions. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of these measures depends upon both the soil characteristics and the current SOC content. The project implements one or more new changes to conventional farming practices, which: a) Improved fertiliser (organic or inorganic) management; b) Improved water management/irrigation; c) Reduces GHG emissions; The project was initiated in Odisha. The first project activity was implemented on 51.80 hectares in the Ganjam and Bhadrak Districts. The project intends to implement a broad range of activities that decrease net emissions of CH4 and N2O from rice farming operations compared to the baseline scenario. This will contribute strongly to the sustainable development of rural villages in the project areas.

Kerry Group is launching the Improved Agriculture and Land Management Project as part of its wider Group sustainability strategy in agriculture in Ireland. Kerry Group is the world's leading taste and nutrition company, bringing technology leadership and sustainable growth to the food and beverage industries. The Project will deliver verified GHG reductions within Kerry’s supply chain network, containing 3000 farmers via the reduction and implementation of sustainable fertiliser practices. The project implements Agricultural Land Management (ALM) project activities that reduce net nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions from agricultural cropping systems by reducing and sustainable application of the nitrogen (N) fertiliser application rate compared to the business as usual (BAU) scenario. During the project crediting period, the Project will adhere to ‘Best Management Practices’ (BMPs) as they relate to applying synthetic and organic N fertiliser at the project sites as required. These BMPs relate to N fertiliser formulation (or N content of organic additions), dates, and application methods. The project will target the reduction of GHG emissions from nitrogen fertiliser applications (urea and calcium ammonium nitrate). The project activity owners (or project instance sites) are 3000 Kerry farmers that are currently supplying KERRY with dairy products for milk production in 7 counties located south-west of Ireland, operating on a total of 177,000 ha of land.

The eAgronom Project for the Improvement of EU Soils Health is an Agricultural Land Management (ALM) carbon project developed and owned by eAgronom to implement project activities in any member country of the European Union. It follows Verra’s VM0042 methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management, version 2.0. The Project is dedicated to enhancing soil organic carbon levels in arable lands, perennial croplands, and permanent grasslands. Its primary goal is to encourage the adoption of regenerative agricultural practices that foster carbon sequestration while minimizing and eliminating greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.

This project will take place on farms primarily in the Kasungu District of Malawi. All the involved farms are managed (and owned or leased) by Press Agriculture Limited (PAL). The project will begin with 4,000 acres of farmland and this could scale up over the duration of the project. The purpose of this project will be primarily to increase soil-based carbon sequestration, without decreasing the productivity of the involved farmland. The PAL farms will introduce the following interventions to meet these goals: improving agroforestry (and crop planting) through the planting of Msangu trees (either as boundary trees or on fallow land) and the establishment of a liaison to support all the farms involved in this project. This project will utilize the VCS Methodology VM0042 (Version 2.0), Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management. This project will use VM0042’s Quantification Approach 2: Measure and Re-Measure. Soil sampling will be used to measure soil carbon. Teralytic’s probes will simultaneously be used to measure the levels of soil carbon, and to corroborate the results of soil sampling. The use of Teralytic’s probes will be supplemental to the methodology’s requirements. The project is expected to generate greenhouse gas emission reductions and carbon dioxide removals of 10,000 tons for the first 4,000 acres. In subsequent years, as the total farmland scales up, the expected reductions could also increase, with 10,000 tons being the lowest threshold of greenhouse gas emission reductions.

The Carbon Credit Ukraine Initiative is a collaborative project initiated in Ukraine between Lithuanian company UAB Heavy Carbon and Ukrainian farmers. The project promotes improved agricultural land management practices to create a long-term shift towards climate change mitigation and biodiversity-friendly farming methods. UAB Heavy Carbon strives to assist farmers in surmounting obstacles that hinder the adoption of improved sustainable land management practices. The project proponent aims to expand its project to encompass diverse conservation-focused farming methods throughout Ukraine through financial assistance, scientific knowledge, training, and technical support. Ultimately, the goal is to shift from conventional agricultural practices to more robust, resilient and sustainable agrifood production systems.

This project unites 106 farmers, including landowners and tenants, organized under various producer associations across 158,000 hectares in Uruguay. Its primary aim is to promote Holistic Management (HM) and regenerative practices in livestock systems, facilitating soil organic carbon sequestration on properties primarily used for extensive livestock farming.

Agoro Carbon Brazil Program is a grouped VCS project implemented by Agoro Carbon Alliance. The program will implement a package of regenerative agricultural land management activities as prescribed in the VM0042 methodology. The implementation of these practices will lead to increases in carbon sequestration rates in the soil as well as a host of other co benefits. The main objective of the program is to provide the financial, agronomic and educational support needed for growers to adopt new farming practices that not only produce agricultural products in a sustainable and profitable way, but also have a positive impact on climate change.

Project Description:The Rivulis Climate Sustainable Orchards in the Iberian Peninsula (RCSO) grouped project aims to create a new sustainable farming approach for olive groves and tree and nut orchards in the Iberian Peninsula. The first instances of the project are in Portugal, we expect to add more instances in Portugal and Spain. The three main goals of this project are as follows, first to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from farming by reducing on-farm energy consumption through the adoption of more efficient irrigation methods such as micro-irrigation coupled, when possible, with more efficient energy sources and by decreasing usage of synthetic fertilizers through the use of fertigation solutions and organic fertilizers, secondly, Increase carbon storage in soils through the implementation of soil conservation practices such as Cover crops and/or inter-crops, tillage reduction and incorporation of tree pruning residues in soils and lastly by increasing carbon storage in the woody biomass by the plantation of native olive groves and fruit, nuts and tree orchards. The baseline conditions of our project are defined as conventional row crops and intensive farming resulting in high greenhouse gas emissions from inefficient irrigation methods such as central pivots, intensive use of synthetic fertilizers, and limited focus on carbon sequestration in soil and soil health. This is due to extensive tillage; minimal incorporation of crop residues into the soil, limited adoption of cover crops and intercrops, and little to no woody biomass. The project is led by Rivulis Climate, as part of a global initiative developed by Rivulis Pte. Ltd, a leader in irrigation solutions, that supports the agriculture transition to more sustainable farming practices. The project is developed according to VCS methodology - VM0042 Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management V2.0 - and falls under VCS Sectoral Scope 14, AFOLU.

The PROCarbono Project, initiated by Bayer Crop Science in Latin America, facilitates the adoption of regenerative agricultural practices and the optimization of inputs through innovative supportive tools that provide essential technical awareness. These tools enable growers to receive tailored management recommendations based on their baseline and edaphoclimatic factors, ultimately aiming for significant reductions and removals of greenhouse gas emissions. Utilizing remote sensing technology, the project effectively monitors crop planting, harvest cycles, and soil coverage, identifying key opportunities for enhancing carbon sequestration. The initiative has already monitored fields across four of Brazil's six biomes and in 15 states, focusing on improvement of Agricultural Land Management (ALM) and carbon stock assessments to deepen understanding of soil organic carbon dynamics in tropical and subtropical climates. Over the project's duration, participating growers are encouraged to expand these sustainable practices to additional areas of their farms. Given the rapid dynamics and challenges posed by climate change, the project emphasizes the gradual implementation of resilient practices supported by digital agriculture tools. By fostering a year-by-year transition, these combined practices aim to enhance both carbon stocks and overall crop productivity, contributing to a more sustainable agricultural future in Brazil.

The Western American Rangelands Regeneration project aims to remove greenhouse gases from the atmosphere by implementing adaptive multi-paddock grazing on numerous ranches across the American West. It is a grouped projected starting with over 80,000 acres in the first instances. AMP grazing allows for the rest and rotation of pastures that have been historically overgrazed and the restoration of perennial and desirable grass species, thus leading to greater carbon inputs into the soil.

This grouped project promotes sustainable grazing across Colombia’s diverse ecosystems, including the Llanos Orientales and inter-Andean valleys. Decades of overgrazing have degraded grasslands, causing soil erosion, compaction, and nutrient depletion, which reduces pasture productivity. This project supports the local ranchers in adopting practices such as rotational grazing, pasture enhancement, and improved livestock genetics suited to local conditions. Additionally, it promotes silvopastoral systems that integrate trees to boost carbon sequestration and discourage overgrazing, burning, and logging. The project will be implemented with the collaboration of field partners, who will help transfer knowledge and incentivize better ranching practices. The carbon finance resulting from this project is also expected to incentivize the implementation of the project activities. We estimate an initial yearly GHG removal of 700,000 tCO2e using the VM0042 methodology, version 2. The number of ranchers participating in the program is also projected to grow over the course of the crediting period. The project aligns with SDGs 2, 6, 8, 13, and 15, aiming for broad impact across Colombia’s grassland regions.

NaturAll Carbon Limited presents the NaturAll Carbon Program – Regenerative Agriculture in Brazil – Project II, a transformative initiative covering 253,128,708 hectares across 13 Brazilian states within the Cerrado and Amazon ecotone. Recognizing that inadequate agricultural management practices are primary drivers of high greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and soil degradation, this project addresses the critical need for effective programs that support farmers in transitioning to regeneration-focused soil management. Launched on January 1st, 2022, the project implements regenerative agricultural practices that are not common in the region, ensuring additional environmental benefits. These practices aim to reduce and remove GHG emissions from the atmosphere, increase Soil Organic Carbon (SOC), and prevent physical, chemical, and biological soil degradation. By enhancing soil fertility and productivity, the initiative also improves resilience to extreme weather events, ensures food security, and preserves natural resources along with their ecosystem services. The program plans to expand over time, engaging multiple stakeholders across diverse agricultural and livestock activities. By fostering resilient and sustainable agropastoral systems in the Cerrado and Amazon ecotone region, NaturAll Carbon Limited is committed to driving positive environmental outcomes.
