Life Climate Soil Carbon Project in Turkiye (referred to as the 'Project' hereafter) is developed by Life İklim ve Enerji Ltd. Şti. to implement activities aimed at reducing agricultural greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. It utilizes the VM0042, Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management. The project's goal is to increase farmers' understanding of the advantages of sustainable agriculture and raise their awareness to modify their agricultural methods to contribute to mitigating and adapting to climate change. Life Climate Soil Carbon Project in Turkiye aims to decrease emissions resulting from agricultural practices and enhance the storage of carbon in the soil. The Program will implement a package of regenerative agricultural land management activities. The project activities are the following: • Tillage and/or residue management • Crop planting and harvesting (e.g. crop rotations) • Fertilizer (organic) application management • No-plough cultivation The baseline farming practices, characteristic of conventional agriculture, typically involve intensive tillage methods, including ploughing and cultivation during planting and weed control, often leaving the soil exposed. These practices can lead to the degradation of Soil Organic Carbon (SOC), which may result in the increased use of synthetic chemical inputs to maintain crop production and yields. Over time, this reliance on chemical fertilizers and pesticides can further degrade soil health and sustainability. Life Climate Soil Carbon Project in Turkiye is a grouped project. The project is located in Turkiye (İzmir, Aydın, Manisa, Denizli, Şanlıurfa). The project will cover 4,956.43 ha. The project is expected to expand to an area in the provinces of same locations and Kahramanmaraş in the coming years.

The project will recruit Prince Edward Island farmers to adopt low-carbon management practices on their farms that will result in GHG emission reductions and removals. These practices include one or more of the following measures: ● Cover Cropping—the seeding of cover crops before and after cash crops to increase the amount of time soil is covered and living roots are active. ● Reduced Tillage—adoption of minimal tillage and soil disturbance to reduce Carbon losses and increase soil aggregation which promotes increases in soil organic carbon ● Improved Rotations and Increased Perennials—altered crop rotations by lengthening or substitution to allow more time for perennial root growth. ● Improved Nitrogen Management—lower fertilizer use, application efficiency practices, and use of alternative fertilizer products. ● Improved Grazing Practices—implementation of intensive cell grazing practices to maximize perennial herbaceous biomass and Carbon inputs to soil. Extensive research confirms that these low-carbon management options promote root growth, increase soil organic carbon and lower the need for fertilizer inputs, leading to significant reductions in nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions . Reduced tillage and cover crops also increase nutrient use efficiency and reduce N2O emissions.
Irrigation upgrades for multiple crops in several regions including Turkey to address methane and NO2 avoidances and soil carbon sequestration.

The Seeds of Recovery: The Ukrainian Regenerative Agriculture & Carbon Removal Program is an Agricultural Land Management project developed and owned by Sentinel Earth aiming to enhance soil organic carbon levels and decrease farm's GHG footprint. In context of severe impacts of Russian military invasion we aim to bring funding incentives and knowledge for affected entities to modernize their technology and practices and build back Ukrainian agriculture better.

“The regenerative and eco-oriented agriculture project in Ukraine” is the first initiative entirely developed and managed by Ukrainian team to support national farmers in adopting eco-friendly and regenerative agricultural practices. Aligned with the Agricultural Land Management (ALM) category and Verra’s VM0042 (v2.1) methodology, this project focuses on improving soil health, increasing carbon sequestration, and reducing greenhouse gas emissions. By transitioning from traditional farming methods to regenerative approaches, the project aims to enhance soil quality while contributing to global ecological balance through improved carbon storage and strengthened resilience to the impacts of climate change. The Carbonex team provides comprehensive support to participating farmers, including consultations, training and technical assistance. Collaboration with the National University of Life and Environmental Sciences of Ukraine ensures the implementation of best practices tailored to local conditions. Beyond its environmental benefits, the project strengthens the economic sustainability of Ukrainian agricultural communities.

The CoolPath Veles California Rangeland Ecological Restoration Project aims to restore degraded rangeland ecosystems across California, addressing the widespread ecological damage caused by invasive annual grasses, altered fire regimes, and overgrazing. Using the Verra VM0042 methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management, the project implements sustainable land management practices, including the application of Title 14-compliant compost, improved grazing management, and re-seeding of native plants. These measures are designed to enhance soil organic carbon levels, improve soil quality, and restore the biodiversity and functionality of California’s rangelands. The primary intervention involves applying Title 14-compliant compost to degraded soils to increase soil organic carbon, stabilize soil structure, and improve water retention and nutrient availability. The compost application also provides a sustainable use for organic waste, aligning with California's Senate Bill 1383, which mandates the diversion of organic waste from landfills. Compost application not only prevents methane emissions from organic waste disposal but also enhances soil health, promoting the growth of native perennial grasses that have been displaced by invasive annual species over the past 300 years. This approach is supported by extensive scientific research, which demonstrates the long-term stability of carbon sequestered in rangeland soils through compost application. The degradation of California’s rangelands has been driven by historical factors, including overstocking of livestock during the California Gold Rush and the introduction of non-native grasses. These invasive grasses, characterized by shallow root systems, outcompete native perennial grasses, reducing soil stability and productivity. This project seeks to enhance key climate indicators, such as soil carbon sequestration and emission reduction, in woody crop farms located within the Mediterranean basin. These farms currently employ conventional management practices characterized by the export of plant residues, bare soils, minimal organic matter application, and frequent tillage. Such practices contribute to soil degradation, increased greenhouse gas emissions, and a decline in biodiversity. However, this scenario also presents a unique opportunity to improve agroecosystems by implementing sustainable management practices. Through the systematic adoption, monitoring, and reporting of these practices, the project will gather valuable data that supports both the scalability of these interventions and their positive environmental impact. Continuous monitoring and adaptive management will ensure ongoing improvement, while financial support will be provided to farms via the generation of carbon credits. These credits can be used to offset residual emissions from corporate activities, helping to meet ambitious net-zero targets. In addition to mitigating environmental impacts, the project will foster biodiversity restoration and promote social benefits by strengthening local agricultural systems, improving farm resilience, promoting effective knowledge transfer and creating new economic opportunities for rural communities.

The project activity aims to promote sustainable and resilient agricultural practices in Kenya’s arid and semi-arid lands (ASALs), which are increasingly affected by land degradation, erratic rainfall, and nutrient depletion. The project encourages the adoption of climate-smart agriculture (CSA) practices such as organic farming, conservation tillage, agroforestry, crop rotation, and residue management. These practices are designed to enhance soil health, improve biodiversity, and optimize farming systems, leading to increased productivity and sustainability. By transitioning from conventional farming practices that rely heavily on chemical inputs, the project seeks to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, restore soil organic carbon (SOC) levels, and support global climate goals. This initiative not only strengthens food security but also enhances the climate resilience of smallholder farmers, providing a scalable model for sustainable agriculture in resource-constrained regions.

This project involves the shifting of irrigation water management in rice cultivation in An Giang Province, Vietnam, implementing the Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) method instead of continuous flooding (CF). Vietnam has 7.0 Mha of rice paddy fields with a total production of 42.6 Mt in 2023, making Vietnam the world’s 5th largest rice producer. Rice cultivation, on the other hand, is a substantial source of greenhouse gasses (GHG) through the emission of methane (CH4). Specifically in Vietnam, it is estimated that rice cultivation is responsible for up to 48% of greenhouse gas emissions and 75% of CH4 emissions in agriculture. Additionally, rice cultivation consumes most of the irrigation water in agriculture, as previous studies have shown it consumes 34 to 43% of the total agricultural irrigation water. One of the solutions to improve water productivity and decrease methane gas emissions in lowland rice production is the implementation of AWD, a water-saving irrigation measure. In AWD, the time intervals between dry and wet circumstances aid in the shift from aerobic to anaerobic soil conditions, resulting in a considerable reduction in methane output. As a result, the project adopts the AWD approach to minimise CH4 emissions. This will also result in a reduction in water use, lowering the farmer's input costs. As a scenario prior to the execution of the project, the farmers in the project area are following the traditional continuous flooding method, which results in significant CH4 emissions due to the anaerobic decomposition of organic matter in the soil. The project proponent along with local partners held training sessions and meetings with farmers to educate them on the benefits of using AWD, which is followed by the installation of AWD pipes in the fields of registered farmers. The expected annual average emission reductions of the project area are 590,682 t-CO2eq, with a total GHG emission reduction of 24,134,780t-CO2eq.

The Green Mpumalanga Project (GMP) is a large-scale ecosystem restoration initiative focused on rehabilitating degraded grassland and savanna ecosystems across 26 nature reserves in Mpumalanga Province, South Africa, spanning over 200,000 hectares. The project tackles degradation from overgrazing, uncontrolled fires, and illegal mining—which have led to biodiversity loss, declining soil organic carbon, and increased erosion—thereby reducing ecosystem resilience to climate change. GMP implements a structured grazing and fire management programme to improve ecosystem functionality and enhance carbon sequestration. Key interventions include: (1) rotational grazing systems that allow vegetation recovery and enhance soil stability; (2) firebreak establishment and controlled burning regimes to lower wildfire intensity and frequency; and (3) erosion control measures to stabilise soils and promote vegetation regrowth. Complementing these, the Green Beef Initiative (GBI) encourages sustainable, carbon-neutral beef production by incentivising local livestock farmers to adopt regenerative grazing practices that improve pasture conditions and carbon storage, with premium market pricing for compliant products. Designed as a phased, grouped carbon project under the VCS using the VM0032 methodology, the first project instance will be piloted in Songimvelo Nature Reserve, selected for its diverse ecosystems and established community engagement. Subsequent phases will expand interventions to additional reserves based on adaptive management from pilot outcomes. The GMP is projected to sequester up to 300,000 tCO₂e annually and directly supports Sustainable Development Goals related to climate action (SDG 13), land restoration (SDG 15), and sustainable economic growth (SDG 8). It also incorporates Payment for Ecosystem Services (PES) mechanisms to provide financial benefits to local communities.

The project, catalyzed by Afriwild Carbon Developments in partnership with Zuka Private Game Reserve, the wider Munywana Conservancy, and Wild Impact, aims to enhance nature-based carbon sequestration efforts within the Munywana Conservancy and adjoining communal rangelands through targeted interventions in fire management, grazing management, and the restoration of grassland. The project area is an ecologically significant area situated in the Maputaland-Pondoland-Albany corridor, and bordering the World Heritage Site of iSimangaliso Wetland Park. It is characterized by a complex mix of savanna grassland and moist broadleaf woodland, including sandveld woodlands, palm savannas, mixed acacia woodlands, mixed Lebombo woodlands, floodplain grasslands, and riparian forests. The project area encompasses sections of the iSimangaliso Key Biodiversity Area (KBA), the Pongolapoort KBA and the Thanda – Manyoni KBA. Within the core project area, 22% constitutes threatened ecosystems in urgent need of restoration and protection, thereby contributing to Targets 2 and 3 of the Global Biodiversity Framework. Land-uses in the project area include private and state wildlife areas, extensive livestock faming and croplands. However, these livelihoods are under threat as, over the baseline period, woody and invasive plant encroachment has led to a net loss of grassland ecosystem and degradation of at least 24% of grassy habitats, resulting in a loss of biodiversity, water retention, and grazing potential. This has catalyzed overgrazing as grass forage decreases, reinforcing a poverty trap in communities that rely on grassland ecosystem services . Ecotourism enterprises in the area are also being diminished as woody encroachment reduces game viewing potential and homogenises habitats. Both woody encroachment and overgrazing negatively impact soil carbon stocks.

The project promotes to enhance agricultural sustainability by implementing a variety of eco-friendly practices. It focuses on transitioning from inorganic to organic fertilizers, incorporating green manure and compost, and minimizing water usage through efficient management techniques. Reduced tillage and no-till practices will help preserve soil structure, while proper crop residue management will prevent burning and promote soil health. Agroforestry will be incorporated to boost biodiversity and carbon sequestration. Additionally, the project will assist farmers with market linkages and fair pricing. These initiatives aim to mitigate climate change, improve soil fertility, and support long-term agricultural sustainability. Over the next 40 years, the project is expected to reduce and remove 76,656 tons of CO2 annually, totalling 3,066,240 tons over its lifetime.

According to baseline surveys, before the implementation of the project, the grasslands in the region were facing severe degradation due to overgrazing, with livestock numbers exceeding the carrying capacity by 1 to 5 times, and the adverse effects of climate variability. These conditions resulted in significant vegetation loss, soil erosion, and depletion of soil organic carbon. The project is aimed to restore the local degraded grassland ecosystem from adoption of sustainable grassland management practices, such as implementing systematic seasonal pasture rotations, limiting the timing and number of grazing animals on degraded pastures, and providing regular training to herders on sustainable grazing practices. Totally, approximately 365,000 ha of degraded pastureland are targeted for restoration through scientifically managed measures. This project quantifies only GHG removals from new project activities using VM0042 methodology, version 2.1. It is estimated to generate an average annual GHG emission removal of 200,000 tCO2e in 40 years. The project contributes to multiple SDGs by creating local jobs (SDG 8), mitigating climate change (SDGs 13), and improving the quality of the grassland and enhancing biodiversity conservation (SDG 15).

AfriScout LLC and Global Communities, in collaboration with local pastoralist communities, are leading the AfriScout Regenerative Grazing Project to address severe rangeland degradation in Southern Ethiopia's Oromia, Somali, and South Ethiopia Regions. This degradation, stemming from overgrazing, climate change, and land use shifts, threatens livelihoods historically reliant on grazing. The project focuses on restoring communal grasslands through community-led adaptive multi-paddock (AMP) rotational grazing, where livestock movements are managed across defined paddocks to allow pasture recovery. This core activity integrates local knowledge with participatory planning, supported by the AfriScout mobile app for monitoring and decision-making. Complementary actions include reseeding, water management structures, and using mobile corrals for soil enrichment. Structured as a grouped project, the project allows expansion to new communities over its 30-year crediting period. The initiative follows the VM0042 methodology for improved agricultural land management, aiming to quantify significant soil organic carbon sequestration and reduce GHG emissions, with initial estimates around 150,000 tCO2e annually. The local pastoralist communities co-design activities and benefit from improved rangelands, enhanced climate resilience, reduced resource conflicts, and shared carbon revenues from the project. The project targets substantial positive impacts on both the environment and local livelihoods, contributing to climate mitigation and adaptation.

The project is in Matad sum, Dornod Province of Mongolia. The project is aimed to restore the local degraded grassland ecosystem from adoption of sustainable grassland management practices, such as implementing systematic seasonal pasture rotations, limiting the timing and number of grazing animals on degraded pastures, and providing regular training to herders on sustainable grazing practices. Totally, approximately 200,000 ha of degraded pastureland is implemented through improved grazing management system. It is estimated to generate an average annual GHG emission removal of 108,000 tCO2e in 20 years.

The project aims to remove greenhouse gases from the atmosphere by implementing regenerative grazing practices in the Ralicó farm, located in the shouthwestern region of the Córdoba province, within the General Roca department in Argentina. The eligible farm area includes both wooded areas and open land. A significant portion is covered by Caldén forest, which shows different levels of density and conservation, while the rest consists of cleared areas, all suitable for grazing management activities. The core strategy of this approach involves subdividing the farm’s large pastures into smaller paddocks and implementing a rotational grazing system. This method ensures that each paddock receives adequate rest and recovery time between grazing periods, promoting healthier soil, improved vegetation cover, and increased carbon sequestration across the landscape

The Three Creeks Grazing Project is an improved grazing project focused on community-led stewardship. The goal of the Three Creeks Grazing Project is to improve riparian conditions and ecosystem services across a watershed-scale landscape, while continuing to support grazing across this multi-jurisdictional rangeland. The project was implemented across 138,000 acres of sage-steppe rangelands in 2022 and resulted in a switch from historical grazing durations and timings to a time-controlled, rest-rotational grazing system. The land included in the project encompasses private, federal (Bureau of Land Management), and state (Utah School and Institutional Trust Lands) ground. The project is located in Rich County, Utah.

The Boomitra Grassland Restoration in Costa Rica project is a grouped initiative supporting ranchers in transitioning from conventional to regenerative, climate-smart grazing practices. Livestock production—covering 35.5% of Costa Rica’s land and employing 12% of the rural workforce—is a key economic sector, but also a major contributor to land degradation and greenhouse gas emissions, accounting for 23.6% of the country’s total. The project addresses financial, cultural, and technical barriers by using carbon finance to enable sustainable practices such as rotational grazing, pasture improvement, silvopastoral systems, and hedgerow integration. These interventions aim to restore soil health, increase productivity, and enhance climate resilience. The project is expected to achieve annual GHG removals of approximately 169,950 tCO₂e, with rancher participation projected to grow throughout. In addition to emissions reductions, the project contributes to multiple Sustainable Development Goals, including SDG 2, SDG 6, SDG 8, SDG 13, and SDG 15.

The project is centered on soil health regeneration through the adoption of improved agricultural land management practices. Its core objective is to support farmers in transitioning to regenerative farming by addressing one of the most critical barriers: access to finance. By leveraging a climate-focused investor community, the project provides affordable financing solutions that enable farmers to maintain profitability while using fewer resources during the transition phase. This support not only empowers farmers to adopt sustainable practices but also enhances their resilience to climate-related events and contributes to the stability of the global food supply chain.

Tourba Improved Agriculture Practices in Nigeria Project is the first of its kind in the country, developed by the Tourba team to support farmers in adopting regenerative agricultural practices. Aligned with the Agricultural Land Management (ALM) category and Verra’s VM0042 (v2.1) methodology, the project aims to improve soil health, increase carbon sequestration, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Beyond its environmental goals, the initiative enhances the economic resilience of smallholder farmers by working closely with them on the ground. It addresses barriers to the adoption of sustainable land management through hands-on training, continuous support, and by building long-term incentives for climate-friendly agriculture — including a fair share of revenues from carbon markets. The project is designed for long-term impact, with plans to scale across diverse farming systems and regions. By empowering farmers and fostering resilient agricultural landscapes, it contributes to both Nigeria’s development goals and global climate action.

NaturAll Carbon Limited presents the NaturAll Carbon Program – Regenerative Agriculture in Brazil – Project IV, a transformative grouped initiative across multiple Brazilian biomes, including the Cerrado, Amazon, Pantanal, and the transition zone between the Cerrado and Amazon. This extensive program reflects a critical response to the urgent need for effective solutions addressing the environmental impacts of unsustainable agricultural practices. Recognizing that poor soil and land management contribute significantly to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and ecosystem degradation, the project implements regenerative agriculture practices that are not yet common in the region. These practices focus on increasing Soil Organic Carbon (SOC), improving soil structure and fertility, and reducing both physical and chemical degradation. As a result, they enhance resilience to climate extremes, promote food security, and preserve essential ecosystem services. The Cerrado, a global biodiversity hotspot, contains 44% endemic plant species among its 10,000 cataloged, while the Amazon harbors half of the world’s terrestrial species and one-third of its tropical rainforests. The Pantanal supports over 4,700 plant and animal species and plays a vital role in the region’s hydrology. The project start date is June 1st, 2022. It uses the VM0042 v2.1 methodology to quantify climate benefits and estimates an average annual removal of 1,562,585 tCO₂e. Over a five-year validation period, the number of participating rural properties is expected to increase, expanding its reach across agricultural and livestock systems. Beyond climate impact, the project delivers key social and environmental co-benefits, including biodiversity protection, rural livelihood support, and the long-term regeneration of Brazil’s most vital biomes.

The proposed Improved Agricultural Land Management (ALM) project aims to to introduce improved agricultural land management practices that reverse land degradation and replenish soil carbon, effectively creating carbon removals and promoting soil health in Nagpur, Maharashtra. The initiative involves improve fertilizer (organic or inorganic) management, Reduce tillage- Minimizing soil disturbance, Improve residue management- Conversion to vermicompost, FYM, compost and improve crop planting and harvesting- Rotational and cover crops introduced in project scenario. The project is developed as a grouped project with a total potential implementation area of 20,000 hectares. In first instance it has enrolled 1,499 smallholder farmers managing a cumulative area of 2,222 hectares for implementation of improved Agricultural Land Management (ALM) practices in Nagpur, Maharashtra .

The group project “Humus Program” supports farms in adopting and implementing organic regenerative agriculture, measuring and certifying carbon sequestration, and restoring soil health and biodiversity—while monetizing these environmental benefits for corporate partners. The project is carried out on existing arable land previously managed using conventional or organic agricultural methods. From the first year, with no transition period, regenerative organic farming practices are implemented. Milpa, the project proponent, is a company founded by a group of French farmers who have spent the past decade developing and refining regenerative organic practices. As of 2025, Milpa deploys these practices across 25 farms spanning 3,255 hectares in northern and western France with a group of technical advisors, deploying these agricultural practices in the field, with the farmers on a day to day basis. More land is expected to join in the coming years, with the goal of reaching 213 000 hectares by the end of the program. Milpa’s system prohibits the use of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides and prioritizes soil health and biodiversity. The system tends toward no tillage and is designed to boost bacterial and mycorrhizal activity, enhancing organic matter decomposition and its transformation into stable humus. This improves soil structure and fertility, enhances water infiltration, and fosters biodiversity—both in the soil and above ground. Carbon stock increases will be measured through soil sampling every three years, both on project plots and on baseline control sites, at depths of up to 1 meter. This follows the “Measure and Remeasure” approach, aligned with the VM0042 methodology. The project aims to remove approximately 100 tCO₂ per hectare over its course. Over time, the project is expected to remove a cumulative total of 14 million tCO₂ from the atmosphere.

The Tourba Improved Agricultural Practices in Brazil is a large-scale carbon initiative promoting regenerative agriculture across 13 Brazilian states with the main focus on the Cerrado biome. Implemented under Verra’s VM0042 (v2.1) methodology and the Agricultural Land Management (ALM) category, the project aims to restore degraded soils, enhance carbon sequestration, and reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions linked to agricultural practices.The project addresses the impact of unsustainable land use by promoting diversified cropping systems and improved pasture management tailored to the specific conditions of each biome. Through site-specific ALM interventions, it delivers both climate mitigation and increased landscape resilience. Its primary objective is to increase soil organic carbon (SOC) and reduce net emissions of CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O from croplands and degraded pasturelands.Beyond its environmental impact, the project strengthens local farming communities. It offers continuous field support and capacity-building to ensure long-term adoption of climate-smart practices. Participating farmers and ranchers receive a significant share of revenues from the sale of high-integrity carbon credits, creating meaningful financial incentives for sustainable land management.By enabling farmers and ranchers and restoring ecosystem function, the project contributes to Brazil’s climate goals and supports global efforts toward a more sustainable and resilient agricultural.

The project is located in Asgat, Dariganga, Ongon, and Naran sums, Sukhbaatar Province of Mongolia. The project is aimed to restore the local degraded grassland ecosystem from adoption of sustainable grassland management practices, such as implementing systematic seasonal pasture rotations, limiting the timing and number of grazing animals on degraded pastures, and providing regular training to herders on sustainable grazing practices. Totally, approximately 300,000 ha of degraded pastureland are targeted for restoration through scientifically managed measures. It is estimated to generate an average annual GHG emission removal of 162,000 tCO2e in 20 years. The project contributes to multiple SDGs by creating local jobs (SDG 8), mitigating climate change (SDGs 13), and improving the quality of the grassland and enhancing biodiversity conservation (SDG 15).

The project is located in Tov Province of Mongolia. The project is aimed to restore the local degraded grassland ecosystem from adoption of sustainable grassland management practices, such as implementing systematic seasonal pasture rotations, limiting the timing and number of grazing animals on degraded pastures, and providing regular training to herders on sustainable grazing practices. Approximately 270,000 ha of degraded pastureland are targeted for restoration through scientifically managed measures. It is estimated to generate an average annual GHG emission removal of 200,000 tCO2e in 20 years.

The project activity supports the adoption of climate-smart agriculture practices among farmers in South Africa by facilitating access to carbon finance. It incentivizes sustainable land management by linking farmers to carbon markets, enabling them to earn revenue for climate-positive actions on their farms. The initiative contributes to emission reductions, improves soil health, and enhances the long-term resilience of farming systems, while aligning with broader global climate goals and strengthening rural livelihoods.

The Brazilian Citrus Program for Climate Adaptation aims to convert lower-productivity and degraded pasture areas into productive citrus orchards by promoting sustainable agricultural practices, such as cover cropping and efficient water irrigation systems. These practices are designed to enhance carbon removal from soil and biomass, while improving the resilience of citrus farming to climate change. Over the next 25 years, the program intends to remove 2,331,500 tCO2e, managing approximately an area of 30,000 hectares. The combined effects of record-high temperatures and spread of greening disease caused by bacteria Huanglongbinh (HLB), have required farmers to relocate to areas with different challenges, mainly within the Brazilian Cerrado. Although the incidence of greening remains low in these new areas, farmers might face additional risks due to acidic soils and less favorable rainfall patterns. Brazil accounts for approximately 35% of worldwide orange production and 75% of international orange juice trade, therefore the development of an even more resilient and sustainable Brazilian citriculture represents a safeguard to food security worldwide. The program seeks to coordinate efforts and promote sustainable agricultural practices to ensure an even more resilient citrus industry. This initiative aims to promote the adaptation to the new climate context while addressing current agricultural challenges.

The Lam Son Regenerative Sugarcane Project is an Agricultural Land Management (ALM) initiative under Verra Methodology VM0042. The project operates as a grouped project covering 508.5 hectares in Thanh Hóa Province, Vietnam. It aims to transition conventional sugarcane cultivation—characterized by high synthetic nitrogen use (up to 350 kg N/ha) and residue burning—to a regenerative, soil-restoring model. Key project activities include: (1) reducing synthetic nitrogen fertilizer to a target of 205 kg N/ha; (2) applying organic amendments such as manure and compost; (3) ceasing post-harvest residue burning in favor of mulching; (4) extending the ratoon-cycle to reduce tillage frequency; and (5) applying lime for soil acidity adjustment. These measures are designed to sequester soil organic carbon (SOC) and reduce N₂O emissions, thereby generating significant annual emission reductions and removals while improving soil health and farmer livelihoods.

The Karoo Sustainable Landscapes Program (KSLP) is a large-scale soil restoration project in South Africa's Western Cape Province. The project targets livestock and biodiversity conservation across three distinct habitat areas: the wet coastal Garden Route belt, the semi-arid Klein Karoo ecosystem, and the arid Groot Karoo ecosystem. The project aims to remove approximately 938,333 tons of CO2e annually through enhanced soil carbon sequestration. This will be achieved through improved grazing and fire management practices, and rangeland restoration across a planned area of 1 million hectares. The project will scale up progressively, starting with 50,000 hectares in 2025 and reaching full implementation by 2028. KSLP operates in the Cape Floristic Region, the world's smallest but second most biodiverse vegetation kingdom after the Amazon. This region hosts over 9,000 plant species, with 70% being endemic. The project's activities include implementing controlled burning protocols, systematic grazing rotation, strategic wildlife population management, and vegetation restoration. Beyond environmental benefits, KSLP aims to improve community livelihoods for 50,000 people, primarily from historically disadvantaged communities. The project works across different land tenure regimes, including private landowners, communities, and government agencies.

The project is located in Akmola Oblast in northern Kazakhstan, which is one of the country's important agricultural areas, mainly used for grain production, especially wheat cultivation. However, due to long-term traditional farming practices, the region faces serious problems such as soil degradation, wind and water erosion, and loss of soil organic matter. Traditional farming practices include continuous cropping systems (such as monoculture of wheat), deep tillage, bare fallow, and monoculture.

The KwaZulu-Natal Sustainable Landscapes Program (KZNSLP) is a grouped project located in the globally significant Maputaland-Pondoland-Albany biodiversity hotspot of South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal Province. The area has experienced significant ecosystem degradation and soil carbon loss due to unsustainable agricultural practices, commercial forestry impacts, and inadequate wildlife management. The project aims to regenerate 1,000,000 hectares of degraded land by 2065 through the implementation of controlled burning protocols, systematic grazing rotation, strategic wildlife population management, and vegetation restoration. KZNSLP integrates biodiversity conservation with sustainable land management across diverse ecosystems, including forests, grasslands, wetlands, and coastal habitats. The region hosts over 8,100 plant species, with 23.5% being endemic, and provides critical habitat for 14 critically endangered, 36 endangered, and 52 vulnerable species, including the iconic Big Five. Working across various land tenure regimes, including private game reserves, communities, and government protected areas, KZNSLP creates a framework for sustainable landscape management while contributing to South Africa's climate change commitments through collaboration with prominent NGOs such as WildTrust, Peace Parks Foundation, and Conservation Outcomes. The project further builds relations by working with traditional authorities as project entities and government agencies who control large land units in the region.

The agricultural sector is a backbone of Ghana’s countryside, employing a majority of the rural population and serving as a critical foundation for food security and climate resilience. In the Upper West Region—where the Nadowli-Kaleo District is located—agriculture provides livelihoods for approximately 85% of the working population, making it the dominant economic activity1. However, traditional agricultural practices—characterized by inefficient fertilizer use, conventional tillage, and frequent burning—have led to extensive land degradation, biodiversity loss, and diminished resilience against climatic variability2. These challenges are particularly pronounced in the savanna ecosystems of the region, underscoring the urgent need for sustainable agricultural transformation and improved land management practices3. The Nadowli-Kaleo Climate Smart Agriculture Carbon Project aims to implement improved agricultural land management (ALM) practices to enhance and protect savanna ecosystems in the Nadowli-Kaleo District of the Upper West Region, Ghana. This initiative, involving smallholder farmers across approximately 45,000 hectares, will significantly increase soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration and above-ground woody biomass through optimized nutrient management, improved soil conservation practices, and sustainable vegetation management adapted to the region’s unique ecological context. The project will introduce a combination of practices specifically aligned with Verra’s VM0042 methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management v2.1, including optimized fertilizer application, integration of organic fertilizers such as manure and compost, implementation of precision irrigation techniques, adoption of reduced or conservation tillage practices, and significant emission reductions and removals in shrub burning and tree cutting4. By optimizing nutrient inputs and adopting improved tillage practices, the project will reduce soil disturbance and erosion, enhance water retention, and improve overall soil health. Precision irrigation ensures efficient water use, thereby supporting sustainable agricultural productivity, even in the context of variable rainfall. Additionally, reducing shrub burning and tree cutting will protect and enhance above-ground woody biomass, providing critical support for biodiversity, hydrological stability, and carbon storage. Before project implementation, agricultural and ecological practices in the Nadowli-Kaleo District were characterized by suboptimal fertilizer use, conventional tillage methods, inefficient irrigation, frequent shrub burning, and unsustainable tree harvesting,collectively contributing to land degradation, soil erosion, reduced agricultural productivity, biodiversity loss, and diminished resilience to climatic stresses. The project is expected to generate an average of 211,923 tCO₂e/year in verified emission reductions and removals annually, delivering measurable climate benefits while contributing directly to multiple Sustainable Development Goals. It supports SDG 13 (Climate Action) by enhancing carbon sequestration, SDG 15 (Life on Land) by restoring degraded savanna ecosystems, SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation) through improved water-use efficiency, and SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) by increasing the share of land under sustainable, resilient agriculture. These outcomes will be achieved through regenerative land management practices, robust community engagement, and science-based monitoring in line with Verra’s VM0042 methodology.

The Soil Center Carbon Initiative (VCS ID: 5710) is a grouped AFOLU project under the Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) using methodology VM0042 (v2.1) for Improved Agricultural Land Management (ALM). Open to regenerative producers who are members of The Soil Center in Washington State, the project began on 1 September 2022 with a 20-year crediting period and renewal provisions under VCS v4.7. The project mitigates greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and enhances soil carbon sequestration through practices such as cover cropping, organic amendments, no/strip tillage, improved water management, rotational grazing, and integrated crop-livestock systems. These measures increase soil organic carbon (SOC), improve input-use efficiency, and reduce emissions from fertilizer and fuel use. The baseline scenario reflected conventional intensive farming: limited or absent cover crops, high chemical fertilizer inputs, minimal rotation, intensive tillage, and little to no organic amendments—contributing to soil degradation and low carbon retention. A dual quantification approach is used: (i) SOC is tracked via direct soil sampling and laboratory analysis (Approach 2: Measure and Remeasure), and (ii) emissions from inputs and operations are estimated using default factors and historical records (Approach 3). The project initially covers 39,000 acres, targeting an average annual reduction/removal of ~2,438,383 tCO2e, totaling ~48,767,659 tCO2e over 20 years. The initiative supports UN Sustainable Development Goals: SDG 2: Zero Hunger – improved soil fertility and food security SDG 12: Responsible Consumption/Production – sustainable farming and transparent reporting SDG 13: Climate Action – verifiable GHG reductions and resilience to climate variability Carbon Friendly Solutions Pty Ltd acts as Project Proponent, managing administration. The Soil Center, as Project Owner, coordinates implementation, soil monitoring, and delivery with Project Implementation Partners (PIPs)

The IndHemp Agricultural Hemp Rotation – Montana project introduces industrial hemp as a rotational crop into conventional farming systems across central Montana, USA. By integrating hemp into existing rotations of wheat, barley, canola, corn, and alfalfa, the project enhances soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration, improves soil health, and strengthens the long-term sustainability of farmland. Industrial hemp used in the project complies with U.S. regulations (≤0.3% THC) and is primarily cultivated for fiber and hurd. The crop’s short growing season, high biomass production, and deep rooting system make it particularly suitable for increasing SOC and promoting regenerative agriculture. IndHemp manages cultivation and harvest in collaboration with contracted farmers, while EcoGaia provides technical advisory support and SoilWatch applies advanced remote sensing and modeling for monitoring. The project applies VM0042: Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management, using Quantification Approach 1 (measure and model) and combining soil sampling, RothC modeling, and satellite imagery. Over a 40-year crediting period (2024–2064), the project is expected to generate an average of 47,545 tCO₂e annually, totaling approximately 1.9 million tCO₂e. Expansion is planned from 192 hectares in 2024 to over 15,000 hectares and 120+ farmers by 2032. Beyond carbon benefits, the project supports the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by enhancing soil fertility and biodiversity (SDG 15), improving farm productivity and resilience (SDG 2, SDG 12), and contributing to climate change mitigation (SDG 13). By demonstrating the role of hemp as a viable rotational crop, the project delivers scalable climate, environmental, and agricultural co-benefits while fostering sustainable land management in Montana.

In Ghana’s Upper West Region, agriculture employs about 80% of the rural population and is vital for food security and livelihoods. Farming in Wa West and Daffiama-Bussie-Issah Districts is dominated by smallholders using traditional methods such as intensive tillage, inefficient fertilizer use, shrub burning, and unsustainable tree harvesting. These practices drive land degradation, soil fertility decline, biodiversity loss, and increased vulnerability to climate stressors. Farmers face barriers to adopting sustainable practices, including financial constraints, limited technical knowledge, cultural reliance on traditional methods, and restricted access to modern technologies. Carbon finance provides an opportunity to address these challenges by supporting climate-smart agriculture that boosts soil carbon sequestration, productivity, and resilience while conserving biodiversity. The Improved Agricultural Land Management for Verified Carbon Emission Reduction and Removal in Wa West and Daffiama-Bussie-Issah Districts Ghana Project seeks to improve land management across 91,000 hectares using Verra’s VM0042 methodology. Interventions include optimized nutrient management, conservation tillage, precision irrigation, improved grazing, agroforestry, farmer-managed natural regeneration, and reduced shrub burning and tree harvesting. Field extension teams will ensure training and community engagement. The project is expected to generate 385,080 tCO₂e reductions annually over 40 years while contributing to SDGs on food security, water efficiency, employment, climate action, and land restoration.

The project is aimed to restore the local degraded grassland ecosystem from adoption of sustainable grassland management practices, such as implementing systematic seasonal pasture rotations, limiting the timing and number of grazing animals on degraded pastures, and providing regular training to herders on sustainable grazing practices.

Sukhbaatar Sustainable Grassland Management Project (hereafter as ‘the project’) is located in Sukhbaatar Province of Mongolia. Soil degradation in Lithuania remains a significant concern due to intensive agricultural practices, especially in regions with sensitive or sloping terrain. Agrokoncernas’s Carbon Farming Initiative aims address the environmental pressures affecting ecosystems and the productivity of farmlands, Agrokoncernas UAB is launching a large-scale initiative to transition over 55,000 hectares of privately managed agricultural land to more sustainable practices over the crediting period of 20 years. The project’s core objective is to adopt land management methods that capture atmospheric carbon dioxide while restoring and enhancing soil health. The primary sustainable agricultural activities carried out are crop rotations, reduced tillage, organic farming, cover crops and reduced fertilizer use. The project is expected to have a mitigation impact of 209,333 tCO2e per year.

ReTerra is an impactful strategic partnership and program between Rabobank Brazil, Ruuts by Ovis and Anthesis. It actively promotes the implementation of a set of regenerative practices on agricultural lands at scale in Brazil. The objective of the ReTerra program is to closely assist producers in a paradigm shift that will help them transition towards more sustainable use of the land. By implementing improved grazing practices and improved crop and livestock systems (ICL), producers will enhance the water- and mineral cycles, improve soil cover and biodiversity while sequestering carbon in their soils. The adopted framework is based on the GRASS standard and decades of experience in holistic management that allows the monitoring of progress.

This program introduces water-efficient farming methods for rice cultivation, including Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD), Direct-Seeded Rice (DSR), and Aerobic Rice Cultivation. These techniques help reduce methane emissions by preventing waterlogged conditions and enhancing crop yields. Furthermore, the program encourages farmers to employ sustainable rice production practices such as conservation tillage, appropriate fertilizer use, and managing agricultural waste without burning.

This project will take place on cropland in the Moyamba District of Sierra Leone, on lands of the Kamajei Chiefdom. All the involved cropland is managed and leased by Leone Agriculture Ltd, and is owned by Kamajei Chiefdom, whose Paramount Chief (PC) is PC Fayia Sundifu Brima Sovula IV. The project will begin with 15,000 acres of cropland and this could scale up over the duration of the project. The purpose of this project will be primarily to increase carbon sequestration in soils and woody biomass, while increasing the productivity of the involved cropland. The project area will introduce the following interventions to meet these goals: improving agroforestry through the planting of apple-ring trees (Faidherbia albida) with intercropping of previously grown crops. This project will utilize the VCS Methodology VM0042 (Version 2.2), Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management. This project will use VM0042’s Quantification Approach 2: Measure and Re-Measure. Soil sampling will be used to measure soil organic carbon, and above and below ground woody biomass will be measured using Verra’s recommended CDM A/R tools.

The Regenerative Agriculture Carbon Offsetting Program (RACO) is a grouped project with New Energy Centre Malaysia Sdn. Bhd (NECM) as the project proponent. This grouped project aims to assist farmers in Malaysia, particularly low - income and small - holder farmers, in adopting improved cropland management and regenerative agricultural practices on their own farms. Over time, some agricultural lands in Malaysia have undergone a certain degree of degradation due to anthropogenic factors, environmental conditions, and extreme weather events. Agriculture plays a crucial role in supporting the country's food security as well as the health and welfare of its people. Malaysia has a mainly tropical rainforest climate and tropical monsoon climate. Although precipitation is relatively abundant, it is unevenly distributed. Moreover, affected by climate change, extreme rainfall and drought events occur from time to time, which accelerates soil degradation, significantly reduces soil organic matter, and further decreases soil productivity, thus constraining agricultural productivity and stability. Meanwhile, in pursuit of agricultural output, some farmers have carried out unreasonable agricultural activities, such as excessive deep tillage and over-fertilization, to make up for the decline in land productivity, which has aggravated soil degradation and damaged the farm ecosystem. In this scenario, the RACO project provides a significant opportunity to improve the croplands in the region and restore soil organic matter by providing eligible farmers with microalgae as a substitute for synthetic fertilizer. This initiative not only enables carbon removal but also enhances overall soil health. The grouped project encompasses a series of improved cropland management practices, including reducing tillage depth, adding microalgae as soil amendment, minimizing the use of synthetic fertilizers, applying organic fertilizers, integrating pest management, improving irrigation system

This program introduces water-efficient rice farming methods such as Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD). These approaches reduce methane emissions by minimizing prolonged waterlogged conditions while also improving crop productivity. In addition, the program promotes sustainable rice production techniques, including conservation tillage, appropriate fertilizer use, and managing agricultural waste without burning.

Beetle Regen: Advancing Low-Emission Agriculture through Improved Land Management in Aurangabad, Maharashtra adopts the VCS Methodology VM0042 – Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management (Version 2.2)1 to implement sustainable cotton cultivation practices aimed at increasing soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks and reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in Aurangabad, Maharashtra, India. The project transitions farmers from conventional to a suite of improved land management practices. These include conservation tillage, intercropping with red gram and green gram (90-day cycle), crop residue retention, application of biofertilizers, reduced nitrogen fertilizer use (~75 kg/ha average), and organic amendments such as farmyard manure (>3 t/ha), neem oil (~1 L/ha), and Dashaparni Ark (10–25 kg/ha). These measures enhance soil health, improve nitrogen use efficiency, and significantly increase carbon sequestration in the soil

The AgriCapture Latin America Rice Methane Project will generate emission reductions under VCS Methodology VM0051: Improved Management in Rice Production Systems. The project supports rice growers in Latin America in adopting improved irrigation practices to reduce both greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and water use. Within the project, growers will implement improved irrigation practices. Prior to project implementation, rice growers in the project practiced continuous flood irrigation. Continuous flooding creates an anaerobic soil environment that fosters methane producing microbes (Searchinger & Waite, 2014). Methane emissions rise as the duration of the flooded period increases, due to the buildup of these microbes (Searchinger & Waite, 2014). By introducing periods of drying that allow oxygen to reenter the soil, improved irrigation practices, like single-drainage and alternate wetting and drying (AWD), can significantly reduce methane emissions. Research indicates that AWD lowers methane emissions by 47% while also decreasing water consumption by up to 39% (Gao, 2024; Atwill R. L., 2020). Participating growers may also transition from transplanted rice to direct seeded rice, another improved irrigation practice. Traditional transplanted rice involves rice seedlings being grown in a nursery before being planted in puddled fields (Ishfaq, Akbar, Anjum, & Anwar-Ijl-Haq, 2020). The process requires a prohibitive amount of labor, and puddling the field requires large amounts of irrigation (Ishfaq, Akbar, Anjum, & Anwar-Ijl-Haq, 2020). Additionally, the puddled fields established before planting increases methane emissions due to increasing the period of anaerobic conditions (Reddy, et al., 2025). When compared to transplanted rice, direct seeded rice reduces methane emissions and water consumption by 70% and 8-12% respectively (Reddy, et al., 2025; Ishfaq, Akbar, Anjum, & Anwar-Ijl-Haq, 2020). The project covers approximately 228,237 hectares of cropland in North Kazakhstan Oblast, where wheat, barley, lentil,etc are the dominant crops. It aims to enhance soil organic carbon stocks and reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions through the adoption of conservation agriculture practices. Prior to the project, conventional farming practices in the region were characterized by intensive tillage, heavy reliance on chemical fertilizers.These practices depleted soil organic matter, reduced soil fertility, and contributed to relatively high GHG emissions. Meanwhile, Recent reports indicate that soil degradation is a significant challenge in northern Kazakhstan, where large areas of agricultural land are affected by erosion, organic matter loss, salinization, and declining soil fertility, posing risks to long-term agricultural productivity and sustainability

Future Ecology Improved Agricultural Land Management Project in Aktobe Oblast and North Kazakhstan Oblast and (hereinafter referred to as “the project”) implements improved ALM practices on fields of wheat, barley, and other crops in Aktobe Oblast and North Kazakhstan Oblast, Kazakhstan. The project covers around 83,199 hectares.

The Agricentric Carbon Initiative (“ACI”) is a grouped project implemented by Regenerative Carbon Alliance Ltd (“RCA”), which was founded to empower smallholder farmers in Kenya by partnering with farmer cooperatives (“co-ops”) to scale regenerative agriculture. The Project is developed under VM0042 v2.2 (Improved Agricultural Land Management) and aims to generate greenhouse gas (GHG) emission reductions and removals (“ERRs”) through the adoption and maintenance of improved cropland management practices by participating smallholder farmers. ACI is located in western Kenya and covers approximately 39,854 hectares across five co-ops, including Mumberes, Eor e Maa, Lanyuak, Kipsigis, and Kabianga, spanning parts of Kericho, Bomet, Baringo, and Narok counties. Co-ops are the backbone of Kenyan agriculture, providing an institutional structure for aggregating smallholder participation and supporting implementation through extension services, training, market linkages, and collective access to credit. Since independence in 1963, this model has facilitated the commercialization of smallholder agriculture and remains a core feature of Kenya’s rural economy, with over 25,984 registered in the country. Co-ops are registered under a primary economic activity (e.g., dairy or tea); however, individual member farmers commonly maintain diversified crop production systems in parallel with the cooperative’s primary focus. The Project encompasses multiple cropping systems across participating cooperatives. Mumberes, Eor e Maa, and Lanyuak primarily operate maize-based systems, with limited production of other vegetable crops including peas, carrots, potatoes, and kale. Kipsigis and Kabianga primarily operate tea-based systems, with minor additional production of vegetables and fodder crops. The project promotes conservation tillage, managing crop residues (eliminating burning), and reduced use of synthetic fertilizers.

The Group project of “Improved Agricultural Land Management In CPP Paddy Fields, Thailand” aims to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and enhance carbon dioxide removals through the adoption of improved agricultural practices in rice production. The project is developed under the Verra VM0042 Improved Agricultural Land Management (ALM) methodology for the voluntary carbon market and is designed to generate verified carbon credits while maintaining rice productivity and strengthening the long-term sustainability of agricultural systems. The project will implement a package of improved land management practices, including reduced or minimum tillage by adjusting planting method to limit soil carbon losses; retention of rice residues and/or use of cover crops to increase soil organic carbon inputs and improve soil fertility; and optimized nutrient management by crop requirement and soil testing recommendation particularly nitrogen fertilizer use, to reduce nitrous oxide emissions and improve water and nutrient-use efficiency. Farmer training for adoptional packages and soil health monitoring will support consistent implementation and performance by CPP extension unit. The project will be implemented in Rainfed jasmine rice-growing regions in farms of CPP area of 32,034 ha in Thailand. Final project boundaries located in Si Sa Ket, Surin, Buriram, Yasothon, and Ubonratchathani provinces and participating areas and farmer plots will be defined during detailed project design.

Rice cultivation in continuously flooded paddy fields, as currently practiced in the project area, is one of the dominant anthropogenic sources of greenhouse gas emissions, particularly methane (CH4) emissions. As rice in India is cultivated primarily by smallholder farmers, it is crucial to address these GHG emissions in a multi-stakeholder program with on-the-ground support. Activities and technologies to reduce GHG emissions must be readily available and implementable for smallholders, considering water shortage and potential soil fertility issues as well as labor constraints in these farming systems. The objective of The Good Rice Alliance improved rice production program in India is to address the methane-intensive method of flooded rice cultivation to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by introducing various agricultural practices that contribute to reducing the anaerobic decomposition of organic matter. The project focuses on transitioning rice farms from the conventional method of continuous flooding to the alternating wetting and drying (AWD) technique. AWD introduces controlled irrigation with periodical flooding and monitoring of the water table to ensure soil aeriation while maintaining optimal water supply to ensure full rice yield. In its initial phase, TGRA involves more than 12,000 smallholder farmers who cultivate more than 16,000 hectares of rice fields with one or two rice growing seasons per year. The program is implemented in collaboration with regional partners in all participating states. The program improves the farmers’ livelihoods by reducing their production costs and improving yield, supported by direct payments for participating in the project. Production efficiency gain, yield increase and water savings provide multiple SDG benefits beyond SDG 13, namely contributions to SDG 2 and SDG 6. The estimated net GHG emission reductions from the project are 181,500 tCO2 equivalent per year, over a crediting period of 10 years.

The AgriCapture Southeast Asia Rice Methane Project will generate emission reductions under VCS Methodology VM0051: Improved Management in Rice Production Systems. The project supports rice growers in Southeast Asia in adopting improved irrigation practices to reduce both greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and water use. Within the project, growers will implement improved irrigation practices. Prior to project implementation, rice growers in the project practiced continuous flood irrigation.

The Kenya Highlands Grouped Carbon Project is a grouped agroforestry initiative developed by Sustainable Carbon and AEN Kenya, located in Central Kenya, covering the counties of Kiambu, Murang’a, Nyeri, Kirinyaga, and Embu, and aims to engage up to 12,500 smallholder farmers across a potential area of up to 40,000 hectares through the implementation of regenerative agriculture and agroforestry practices under VERRA methodology VM0042. The project promotes the integration of trees with annual and perennial crops, including the use of nitrogen-fixing species, mulching, composting, and improved organic soil fertility management, increasing tree cover, restoring soil health, and enhancing ecosystem functions. The project is implemented in a region that has experienced significant land degradation due to unsustainable agricultural practices such as slash-and-burn and short cultivation cycles, leading to declining soil fertility, reduced vegetation cover, biodiversity loss, and increasing pressure on natural forests, while negatively affecting smallholder livelihoods. By supporting the transition to diversified agroforestry systems, the project will generate greenhouse gas emission reductions and removals through increased soil organic carbon and aboveground biomass, while restoring degraded lands, improving agricultural productivity, enhancing biodiversity including pollinators, and strengthening climate resilience. The project will initially be implemented over approximately 11,000 hectares, with planned expansion to up to 40,000 hectares by 2033, generating Verified Carbon Units (VCUs) alongside co-benefits such as increased farmer income, improved food security, and more resilient rural communities.

Respira Patagonia is a high-impact Grouped Project focused on Agricultural Land Management (ALM), situated across the vast and iconic landscapes of the Magallanes and Chilean Antarctica Region, including Tierra del Fuego. Utilizing the VM0042 methodology, the project covers an initial phase of 250,000 hectares dedicated to the transition from conventional extensive grazing to Regenerative Livestock Management.The project is designed to tackle the historical degradation of the Patagonian steppe. By implementing planned grazing and rotational models, Respira Patagonia restores the natural carbon-sink capacity of these grasslands. Over its 20-year crediting period, the project is conservatively estimated to remove approximately 17 million tonnes of $CO_{2}e$ from the atmosphere, making it a cornerstone for regional climate action.Key Impact Pillars:Massive Carbon Removals: Targeted sequestration of ~17M tCO2e through enhanced Soil Organic Carbon (SOC) stocks.Ecosystem Restoration: Active recovery of the fragile Patagonian steppe, reversing desertification and improving water retention.Biodiversity Lifeline: By restoring native grasslands, the project provides a thriving habitat for endemic species, ensuring the conservation of Southern Chile unique biological heritage.Scalable Sustainability: As a Grouped Project, it offers a robust framework for local estancias to join the green economy, fostering resilience for rural communities.Respira Patagonia represents a paradigm shift in Patagonian ranching, proving that profitable livestock production can coexist with large-scale carbon sequestration and the preservation of one of the world’s last wild frontiers.

The Venture Carbon Tropical Agricultural Soil Carbon Removal Project is a grouped initiative developed by Venture Carbon Ltda. under the VCS VM0042 v2.2 methodology and VCS Standard v4.7, targeting measurable increases in soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks and reductions in GHG emissions (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O) across consolidated agricultural and grazing lands in Brazil. Classified under Agricultural Land Management (ALM), Sectoral Scope 14 (AFOLU), the project spans a 20-year crediting period (2025–2045) with estimated total removals of approximately 13.9 million tCO₂e. Venture Carbon fully funds every stage of the carbon project lifecycle, from soil sampling and laboratory analysis to certification, third-party audits, credit issuance, and sale, eliminating financial barriers for participating producers. The project is grounded in agronomic science, prioritizing the biological and chemical foundations of productive systems: soil health, microbial biology, and nutrient cycling. By restoring degraded areas and sequestering carbon through improved management practices, including no-till farming, diversified crop rotation, cover cropping, and crop-livestock-forestry integration, the project aligns land recovery with verified carbon removal outcomes. All participating properties must demonstrate full compliance with the Brazilian Forest Code and applicable environmental regulations. Eligibility screening includes geospatial verification through MapBiomas to confirm no native ecosystem conversion occurred within ten years prior to inclusion. As a grouped project, new activity instances may be added over time provided they meet all methodological and regulatory requirements. The project positions Brazilian tropical agriculture as a strategic source of high-integrity, science-based carbon removals in the voluntary carbon market, contributing to multiple Sustainable Development Goals while reinforcing the productive capacity and environmental resilience of participating farms.

The project is an Improved Agricultural Land Management (IALM) initiative implemented under the VM0042 methodology across approximately 20,000 hectares of cropland in Northern Kazakhstan. The project area is primarily used for the cultivation of wheat and sunflower. Under the baseline scenario, agricultural practices consist of conventional crop rotations with fallow periods between cropping seasons. These practices result in exposed soils during non-growing periods, leading to soil organic carbon (SOC) loss, increased erosion, and gradual land degradation. The project introduces cover cropping as the primary intervention, replacing fallow periods with continuous vegetative cover. Cover crops such as winter rye are established following the harvest of the main crop and are not harvested for commercial purposes. Instead, it is terminated prior to the next planting season and incorporated into the soil, contributing to organic matter and improving soil structure. Through these activities, the project enhances carbon sequestration by increasing SOC stocks. Carbon is removed from the atmosphere through plant growth and stored in soils via root biomass and crop residues. Additional benefits include reduced soil erosion, improved moisture retention, and enhanced nutrient cycling. The project is expected to generate greenhouse gas removals primarily from SOC accumulation, with an estimated average of 38,000 tCO₂e per year over the crediting period.

This would be achieved by introducing technically proven initiatives/ techniques which would result in reduction of fresh water consumption and thereby decrease the dependency on application of synthetic fertilizers and other amendments. This Project is being developed as a grouped project across multiple states of India. The PRO Carbono Project in Argentina is a science-based, farmer-centered initiative led by Agro Bayer SRL to accelerate the transition toward regenerative agriculture at scale. Structured as a grouped Agricultural Land Management (ALM) program, the project is implemented across Argentina’s main agricultural regions, covering 11 provinces with diverse productive, soil, and climate conditions. Through Bayer’s agribusiness network, digital platforms, and technical support, participating farmers are enabled to adopt improved land management practices, including enhanced crop residue management, more diversified and intensified crop rotations, the integration of cover crops within three-year production cycles, and optimized input application. These interventions are designed to increase soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks and reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions while preserving productivity and strengthening farm resilience. By improving year-round soil cover, increasing biomass inputs, and enhancing nutrient-use efficiency, the project generates measurable climate benefits alongside agronomic and environmental co-benefits, such as healthier soils, greater system stability, and improved adaptive capacity under lately climate change scenario. PRO Carbono Argentina combines applied science, digital innovation, and practical farm-level implementation to create a scalable pathway for climate-smart agriculture. Its additionality is supported by the opportunity to tune the baseline and support adoption of regenerative practices in the target regions and by the project’s role in helping growers overcome technical, operational, and financial barriers that often limit broader adoption. As a result, the initiative positions agricultural producers as key contributors to climate mitigation, while reinforcing long-term carbon permanence, sustainable productivity, and the transformation of agricultural landscapes into more resilient and lower-emission production systems.

The project, initiated by Agbiotech (Tokyo, Japan) in active operational collaboration with local partner Subhiksha (Bangalore, Karnataka, India), is a climate-smart agricultural initiative designed to systematically reduce methane emissions from smallholder lowland paddy rice cultivation. The pilot phase encompasses a designated 19.5-hectare footprint situated within the anthropogenically irrigated agricultural plains of the Davanagere district in Karnataka, India. The primary objective of the intervention is to establish a verified, scalable digital Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification framework that demonstrates how structural adjustments to traditional water-delivery and irrigation workflows can successfully suppress soil methanogenesis without compromising smallholder crop yields or food security.

The Agreena Kazakhstan Carbon Project reduces agricultural GHG emissions and increases removals through the implementation of project activities rooted in the central principles of regenerative agriculture. The Project intends to support farmers across the northern Kazakhstan grain belt in transitioning to regenerative agriculture by adopting sustainable management practices that maintain yields while ensuring the long-term viability of their land. The technologies and activities to be implemented by project participants, either individually or as a combined suite of practices.

The project is aimed to restore the local degraded grassland ecosystem from adoption of sustainable grassland management practices, such as implementing systematic seasonal pasture rotations, limiting the timing and number of grazing animals on degraded pastures, and providing regular training to herders on sustainable grazing practices. This is a proposed project activity involves implementation of improved water management technique in rice fields which uses less water than the existing system of continuously flooded irrigation in the rice field primarily known as Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) technique across irrigated rice fields, proposed under two regions viz. Haute Matsiatra and Amoron’i Mania of Republic of Madagascar. The traditional practice of continuously flooded rice cultivation is predominantly followed in the host country region which remains the baseline. Flooded rice cultivation is one of the largest anthropogenic sources of methane emission globally, whereas proposed AWD technique is based on intermittent irrigation cycles that allow controlled drainage and re-flooding, the project reduces anaerobic conditions that drive methanogenesis, thereby reducing the (CH₄) methane (GHG) emissions while maintaining or improving yields and water-use efficiency. The project is currently at initial stage of implementation, is estimated to generate average annual GHG emission reductions of approximately 567,000 tCO2e, across an estimated rice cultivation area of 110,000 ha under the two proposed regions. This Malaysian Paddy dMRV Program seeks to implement improved rice cultivation practices in Malaysia under Verra’s VCS Methodology VM0051: Improved Management in Rice Production Systems. The AgriCapture Improved Grazing Project (the “Project”) is a grouped project that implements planned rotational grazing on grazing land in the United States. The first monitoring period includes one project activity instance on approximately 6,634 acres of privately owned grazing land in southwestern Montana, in the area of the Bridger Mountain Range and the Crazy Mountains. The Project’s baseline scenario is continuous grazing, in which cattle graze freely within large pastures for extended, indefinite periods before being moved. Under the Project, ranch managers implement an improved grazing plan that increases livestock stock density and the frequency of pasture rotation relative to the baseline. These practices, commonly referred to as rotational grazing, adaptive multi-paddock (AMP) grazing, or management-intensive grazing (MiG), have been shown to increase the rate of soil carbon sequestration in grassland soils, generating removals over the Project crediting period. The Project start date is 01-September-2023, and the first crediting period runs through 30-August-2043. Average annual estimated GHG emission reductions and removals (ERRs) for the first crediting period are 1,990 tCO₂e, with total estimated ERRs of 23,800 tCO₂e over the 20-year period.
